```text
                         read piped text.  (file or piped
                         stdin; - selects stdin, required)
  -o, --format <format>  Select the output format, records
                         by default. One of: records, json,
                         jsonl.

GLOBAL OPTIONS
  -h, --help        Show this help.
  -V, --version     Print the version.
  -M, --manifest    Print this command's manifest as JSON.
  -e, --explain     Explain the selected command and exit.
      --[no-]color  Turn color on or off, overriding
                    NO_COLOR.
  -v, --verbose...  Show more detail. Repeat it for more.
  -q, --quiet       Hide info and success messages.

EXAMPLES
  $ jsonkit -f doc.json
  $ jsonkit get user.name -f doc.json

Run jsonkit <command> --help for command details.
```

At 30 columns the COMMANDS row set stacks, because its indent, its left column, and its floor, `application's`, need 2 + 22 + 13 = 37 columns:

```text
COMMANDS
  doctor
      Check the host this
      application runs on.
  completion <command>
      Print or install a shell
      completion script.
  mcp
      Serve this application's
      tools to an MCP client
      over stdin and stdout.
  manpage <command>
      Write or install the man
      pages.
```

[ADR-0087](decisions/0087-help-wraps-its-prose-to-the-destinations-columns-and-keeps-its-literals-whole.md) records the decision.

- **Where it applies.** The page lays out against its view context's [`columns`](#width-padding-and-multiline-lanes), the effective width of stdout, where help prints. When `columns` is `undefined`, as on a pipe, a file, an invocation by name, and an MCP tool call, every page is byte for byte the page the rules above print, tabs included. `COLUMNS` narrows the page as it narrows every view. The compact and extended variants follow the same rules. Help wraps at `columns` itself, with no maximum line length of its own.
- **What wraps.** Prose wraps: the masthead description, the message of the `Deprecated:` line under a masthead, every right cell, which is its description, its accepted-values sentence, and its fact parenthesis, read as one text, every Details block except code and a thematic break, the INPUT block's description and its `Required.` or `Optional.` sentence, each option-group sentence, such as `Use at most one of --json and --yaml.`, each example note, and each hint.
- **What stays whole.** Literals never wrap: USAGE forms, outer section titles and inner headings, left cells, Details code, table rows, and thematic breaks, the INPUT block's `Example: <producer> | <path>` line, and example commands with their `$`. One wider than the space left for it overflows, and the terminal soft-wraps it. Inside prose, a Details code span and the command a hint names, such as `jsonkit <command> --help`, sit in [`nowrap`](#width-padding-and-multiline-lanes), so each stays on one line. A link's destination holds no space, so it stays whole as any word does.
- **Breaking.** Every wrap is `context.wrap` at the width left for its text, under its rules: greedy, breaking at U+0020 spaces alone, keeping a word wider than the width whole. Before the view measures, wraps, or indents text, it expands tabs with `context.expandTabs`, so the page holds no tab: a right cell's assembled text once, and each authored line of a Details block from that line's start, before its lines join. The view splits wrapped text with `splitLines` and places each line after its unstyled indent, so a style that spans a break closes before the indent and opens again after it. Where the width left for a text is less than one column, the text prints unwrapped.
- **Hanging indents.** A continuation line starts where its text's first line starts. The masthead description continues under its first character, after `<path> · `, and the deprecation message under its first character, after `Deprecated: `. A right cell continues under the right cell's column, a list item under its text after the marker, as an authored continuation is indented, and a quote after the `> ` that starts each of its lines. An example note continues at the note's indent, an INPUT sentence and an option-group sentence at their two-space indent, and a hint at the left margin. When a hanging text's continuation indent and its floor, the widest unit `wrap` keeps whole in it, measured as a table column's floor is, together exceed `columns`, its continuation lines start at its block's base indent instead, and its first line keeps its place: the masthead description and the deprecation message continue at indent 2, and a list item at its list's own indent, where its marker starts. A right cell stacks instead, under the stacked rows rule below.
- **Two columns.** A row set is the rows that share a left column off a terminal: an outer heading's direct rows, or the rows under one inner heading. Its left column keeps its width, the set's longest left cell plus two spaces, and each right cell wraps at `columns` minus the set's indent and that width.
- **Stacked rows.** A row set's floor is the widest unit `wrap` keeps whole in any of its right cells, measured as a [table](#table) column's floor is. When the set's indent, its left column, and its floor together exceed `columns`, the set stacks. Each row prints its left cell on its own line at the set's indent and its right cell on the lines below, four columns past the furthest-in start of a left cell's text in the set, so a set that holds a long-only option, whose left cell carries four alignment spaces, indents every right cell eight columns past the set's indent, wrapped at what remains. A row with no right cell prints its left cell alone, and no blank line separates stacked rows. Every other row set on the page keeps two columns.
- **Details reflow.** A paragraph's lines join with one space, Markdown's soft line break, and the joined text wraps at the width left after the block's indent and its containers' markers and prefixes. A paragraph in a list item or a quote does the same, and a heading, which is one line, wraps as a paragraph does. Inline constructs are still read per authored line under [Markdown inline text](#markdown-inline-text), so joining changes no styling. Code never reflows or wraps, a thematic break prints as written, and the blank lines between blocks stay the author's. Off a terminal, each authored line stays one page line.
- **What does not change.** `HelpPage`, the view's identity, replacement, styles, escaping, and every content rule above stand, and no page line ends in whitespace. The pack exports no layout helper and no parser. The man page and the manifest are unchanged. The version line neither wraps nor reads the width.

Compared with the page rules before this section, the changed rules are: on a terminal, prose wraps at `columns` with hanging indents, a row set that cannot fit stacks, and Details paragraphs reflow at soft line breaks. Off a terminal, nothing changes.

#### Help wrapping acceptance

Help wrapping is proven when public APIs alone produce these results under Node and Bun, through fixtures whose host reports a fixed stdout width and an `env` with no `COLUMNS`:

- **Example pages.** `jsonkit --help` at 60 columns prints the page above, and its COMMANDS row set at 30 columns prints the stacked block above, byte for byte with color and modifiers disabled. `jsonkit -h` and `textstat --help` each fit 40 and 60 columns. `jsonkit get --help` and `jsonkit select --help` fit 60. At 40, only `get`'s second example command and `select`'s USAGE form, which stay whole, run past it. Every example page and every help golden that runs off a terminal is unchanged.
- **Width.** A page at a width it already fits prints its rows as before. `COLUMNS=60` over a real width of 100 lays the page out at 60, `COLUMNS=150` over 100 lays it out at 100, and `COLUMNS=60` on a pipe changes nothing.
- **Right cells.** A description, an accepted-values sentence, and a fact parenthesis wrap as one text under the right column, in an outer heading's direct rows and under an inner heading, whose indent narrows its width. A row with no right cell carries no padding.
- **Stacking.** A row set stacks exactly when its indent, left column, and floor exceed `columns`, and the next row set keeps two columns. An outer heading's direct rows and the rows under its inner headings stack independently. A stacked right cell wraps at the indent four columns past the furthest-in start of a left cell's text in its set, and a right cell whose unit is wider than that space overflows on its own line. A stacked set that holds a long-only option starts every right cell eight columns past its indent, in an outer heading's direct rows and under an inner heading, so no description starts in a spelling's column, and a stacked set without one starts them four columns in.
- **Literals.** A USAGE form, a left cell, a code block line, and an example command wider than `columns` print whole. A Details code span holding spaces, and a hint's command, never break. A link destination wider than the width keeps its own line.
- **Details.** A paragraph authored across several lines joins and wraps at 40 columns and joins into one line at 200. A list item's continuation hangs after its marker, nested two levels, and a quote's continuation carries `> `. A heading wraps. Code keeps every line as written, and an emphasis pair on one authored line stays styled after the join. Off a terminal, each authored line stays one page line.
- **Table rows.** Consecutive Details lines that start with `|` print one page line each at 24 and at 200 columns, with no join and no wrap, even directly after a paragraph, whose lines still join, and off a terminal every Details value that held a pipe table prints as it did before the rule, a row that continues a list item lazily included.
- **Hanging indents.** At 40 columns a masthead description continues after `<path> · `, a deprecation message after `Deprecated: `, an example note at its indent, and a hint at the left margin, and the version line stays one line. When a masthead description's hang cannot fit, as for `jsonkit manpage generate --help` at 30 columns, its first line stays after the path and the rest continues at indent 2, and so does a deprecation message, while a list item whose hang cannot fit continues at its marker's column, nested too.
- **INPUT and option groups.** At 40 columns the INPUT block's description and its stdin sentence wrap at their two-space indent while its `Example:` line stays whole, an option-group sentence wider than the width wraps at the same indent, and off a terminal each prints as one line.
- **Narrow and tabs.** At a width that leaves less than one column for a text, that text prints unwrapped. A tab inside a description, a Details paragraph, and a code line expands on a terminal, and stays a tab off one.
- **Styles.** Exact themed bytes pin a wrapped right cell whose style spans the break, a wrapped fact parenthesis, a wrapped deprecation message, and a stacked row.

### Formatter

The formatter is `@loomcli/plugins/format`. Its factory `format(settings?)` takes one optional setting, `short`, the short spelling `--format` takes, under the convention of [Plugin settings](#plugin-settings), and with none `--format` has no short spelling. It declares no global option and claims no slot. It ships two views, `json()` and `jsonl()`, one hook that puts `--format` on every Command that declares a [result](#results), one always-on middleware that copies a supplied name into `view`, and two [failure encoders](#failure-encoders), for `application/json` and `application/jsonl`. The plugin owns the encodings and the option; core owns the selection.

```ts
// @loomcli/plugins/format
interface FormatSettings {
  readonly short?: NonNullable<StringOption['short']>; // one ASCII letter, as every option's short spelling is
}
function format(settings?: FormatSettings): Plugin<{}>;
function json<Data>(config?: { map?: (data: Readonly<Data>) => unknown }): View<Data>; // mediaType 'application/json'
function jsonl<Data>(config?: { map?: (data: Readonly<Data>) => unknown }): View<Data>; // mediaType 'application/jsonl'
```

```ts
import { Application } from '@loomcli/core';
import { format } from '@loomcli/plugins/format';
import { help } from '@loomcli/plugins/help';
import { table } from '@loomcli/plugins/table';
import { version } from '@loomcli/plugins/version';

export const textstat = new Application('textstat', { plugins: [help(), version(), format({ short: 'f' })] })
  // ...
  .rows<Row>({
    views: {
      table: table({
        columns: [
          { key: 'count', header: 'COUNT', align: 'right' },
          { key: 'source', header: 'SOURCE' },
        ],
      }),
    },
  })
  .action(countFiles);
```

```text
$ textstat --format json one.txt      # the rows as one JSON array on stdout, warnings on stderr
$ textstat --format yaml one.txt
textstat: Option "--format": Supply one of table, json, jsonl.
$ textstat --format json --metric nope one.txt
{"error":{"code":"invalid-input","exitCode":2,"message":"Option \"--metric\": Expected one of: bytes, words, lines.","hints":["Run \"textstat --help\" to see the usage."]}}
$ jsonkit get --format json user.name -f doc.json
jsonkit: Unknown option "--format". Supply a declared option; prefix a hyphenated path with "./".
Run "jsonkit get --explain" to explain this command.
```

Once [help's failure hint](#helps-failure-hint) lands, `Run "jsonkit get --help" to see the usage.` prints between the sentence and the explain line.

An application whose operators and scripts already type `-f` for the format gives it as the short spelling, and the help row carries it:

```ts
new Application('store', { plugins: [help(), format({ short: 'f' })] });
```

```text
$ store list --help
store list

USAGE
  store list [options]

OPTIONS
  -f, --format <format>  Select the output format, table by default. One of: table, json, jsonl.

GLOBAL OPTIONS
  -h, --help  Show this help.
```

`store list -f json` then selects `json` as `store list --format json` does. The default stays no short spelling, because an application such as jsonkit already spells `--file` as `-f`.

- **Views.** `json()` and `jsonl()` are whole views: under `result<Value>` they receive the value, and under `rows<Row>` core collects the sequence and they receive the array. `map` reshapes what they receive, identity by default. They are bare pack views under [Row views](#row-views), typed by contextual typing inside a `views` record and as the second argument of `out.render`, and stated, `json<Summary>()`, when hoisted. They render as ordinary views with the plugin uninstalled, so a Command that names `json: json()` first prints JSON by default with no `--format` anywhere. `json()` declares the [media type](#media-types) `application/json` and `jsonl()` declares `application/jsonl`, whatever `map` they take and whatever key holds them.
- **Bytes.** `json()` writes `JSON.stringify(mapped, null, 2)` and one newline. `jsonl()` writes one line per element when the mapped value is an array, each `JSON.stringify(element)` and one newline, and one such line otherwise; an empty array prints nothing. `toJSON` is honored and an `undefined`, function, or symbol property is dropped, as `JSON.stringify` does. A value that encodes to nothing, `undefined` at the top, or that `JSON.stringify` throws on, a `bigint` or a cycle, makes the view throw `The value cannot be encoded as JSON. Emit plain JSON data from the action.`, or for `undefined`, `The value cannot be encoded as JSON, because it is undefined. Emit plain JSON data from the action.`, reported through the output-view row of the [Failure contract](#failure-contract). The message carries no engine reason, which differs between runtimes; the thrown error keeps the engine's error as its `cause`. The text is data: each view escapes it through `style.escape` and replaces every character from U+007F to U+009F with its `\uXXXX` escape, four lowercase hex digits, so nothing the [rendering policy](#rendering-policies) would strip or read as a terminal control reaches it, and applies no style, so the bytes are the same under every capability.
- **The hook.** A Command with no result is returned unchanged. On one with a result, the hook appends `json` and then `jsonl` to the `views` record where the record lacks the key, so an author's own `json: json({ map })` or `json: myView` is kept as written and the default is unchanged, then declares the local string option `format` after the author's options, with the short spelling `settings.short` names, or none when it is omitted, `control: true` under [Control options](#control-options), and no default, the description `Select the output format, <default> by default.`, where `<default>` is the declared default at that hook, and a validator that accepts each key and returns the issue `Supply one of <names>.` for anything else. The validator also accepts `ndjson` and transforms it to `jsonl`, unless the record names `ndjson` itself; `ndjson` is an unadvertised alias under [Aliases](#aliases). The validator maps `ndjson` to `jsonl` before it checks the record's keys, so the option's [input schema](#input-schema) is the enum of the record's keys and the unadvertised alias stays out of it. The option is an ordinary local option in every respect: parsed at local placement, on the help page as `--format <format>`, or `-f, --format <format>` under `format({ short: 'f' })`, with its description and its accepted values, under the node's `options` in `inspect()`, reaching the action at run time under `options.format` and absent from its types. The `short` setting's type takes one ASCII letter, and the option it spells meets the ordinary option declarations, under [Plugin settings](#plugin-settings). A key or spelling collision with an option the Command, the Application, or another plugin declares, the chosen short spelling included, is the hook-collision build error, naming the plugin, the Command, and the declaration that already holds the name or spelling, and the developer resolves it; the plugin offers no rename. A plugin whose hook adds a view installs ahead of `format()` if `--format` is to accept its name. The same order lets the description reflect a hook's changed default.
- **The middleware.** `activate: 'always'`, because a hook-declared option cannot activate it. When the routed Command declares a result and [`ownOptions`](#middleware) holds a string under `format`, it assigns that string to `view` and calls `next()`; when the option was omitted it assigns nothing, so an earlier plugin's selection stands. A held fault on another input, a structural one such as `--bogus` and an input-source one such as a configuration file that cannot be read included, leaves `format` in `ownOptions`, so the selection stands for the failure, and the fault is raised at the dispatch boundary unless a later middleware takes over. A `--format` its validator rejected is absent from `ownOptions`, so the middleware assigns nothing and the failure's selection stays as it was, the default view when nothing else selected one: `textstat --format yaml one.txt` is the validator's issue, exit 2, written as text because textstat's default view, `table`, declares no media type, and `--format yaml --help` with help installed after the formatter still prints the page.
- **The failure encoders.** The plugin registers one encoder for `application/json` and one for `application/jsonl`, the media types its two views declare, so a failed run whose selected view is a `json()` or `jsonl()` view writes its [failure form](#the-failure-form) as JSON. Both write the same bytes: one line, `JSON.stringify({ error: form })` with the form's keys in the order `code`, `exitCode`, `message`, `hints`, then one newline, to stderr. Every character from U+007F to U+009F is replaced by its `\uXXXX` escape, four lowercase hex digits, as the views replace it, and no style applies. An author's own view that declares either media type selects the same encoder. `--format` on a Command with no result is the unknown-option error, and `--format` twice or with no value follows the rules every string option follows.

```ts
// src/format/middleware.ts, loaded on every invocation that reaches it
import type { Middleware } from '@loomcli/core';

import type { format } from './plugin.js';

const middleware: Middleware<typeof format> = async (context) => {
  // A hook-declared option, so its value is unknown to the types; it stands under a held fault.
  const selected = context.ownOptions.format;
  if (context.view !== null && typeof selected === 'string') {
    context.view = selected;
  }
  await context.next();
};

export default middleware;
```

#### Formatter example coverage

The formatter increment is proven when textstat installs `format({ short: 'f' })` and jsonkit installs `format({ short: 'o' })`, after `help()` and `version()` and ahead of the example plugin, and public APIs alone produce the transcript above: `textstat -f json one.txt` and `textstat --format json one.txt` print the rows as one indented array with the `--timing` line still on stderr, `textstat --format jsonl one.txt` prints one line per row, `textstat one.txt` prints its table, `jsonkit paths -o jsonl -f doc.json` and `jsonkit paths --format jsonl -f doc.json` print one line per `Entry`, `--format ndjson` prints the same bytes, and `--format json` prints one indented array. `textstat --help` prints the page under [The help page](#the-help-page) with its `--format` row, whose description names the declared default, as specified by the [help restyle](#help-and-version-restyle), and whose [accepted values](#accepted-values) list the view names. `inspect()` reports `['table', 'json', 'jsonl']` on textstat's root and `['list', 'table', 'json', 'jsonl']` on `paths`. The acceptance tests cover both views under both units with an empty array and with a map, a `bigint` and a top-level `undefined` as view faults, U+009B and U+001B inside a string printed as escapes under `color: 'never'` and `'always'` alike, an author-declared `json` kept with its map and position, an author-declared `ndjson` key that the alias no longer serves, `--format yaml`, `--format` on a no-result Command, `--format` twice and with no value, an omitted `--format` leaving an earlier plugin's selection in place, `--format yaml --help` printing the page, the hook-collision error against a local, a global, and another plugin's `format`, `format({ short: 'f' })` putting `-f` on the help row and selecting a view through it, its short spelling colliding with a local option's and with help's `-h`. The lifecycle cases live with the [plugin example coverage](#example-coverage-3): a fixture hook declaring an option the action reads at run time and `request` carries, the hook receiving the root, `result` and `hasAction` read from a hook, two plugins' hooks in order with the later replacing a view, each hook build error, `request` holding values on a valid invocation and `null` under a held fault and on a group, a takeover under a held fault and under a throwing validator exiting 0 with no diagnostic, an always-on wrapper ahead of help reaching help's takeover, the held fault raised at the boundary with its code and rank and ranking ahead of a bad `view`, a run cancelled inside a validator and one cancelled mid-chain resolving the signal's code, `view` starting at the default and `null` on a no-result Command, the last assignment before the boundary winning across two middleware, an assignment after the boundary changing nothing, and each `view` fault raised at the boundary and unobserved under a takeover. The two failure encoders' lines are pinned under [Failure encoders acceptance](#failure-encoders-acceptance), and a fixture middleware reads its own global and hook-declared options from `ownOptions` under a held fault on another input, a validation problem, a validator that throws, an unknown option, and a configuration source that fails alike, and finds an option absent when its validator rejected the option's own value or when the option's own occurrence faulted. Each case runs under Node and Bun.

### Table

The table is `@loomcli/plugins/table`. Its factory `table<Row>(config?)` takes a column list and returns a whole view over the collected rows, `View<readonly Row[]>`, so the same value reaches a `views` record under `rows<Row>` and the second argument of `out.render`. Nothing is installed: there is no plugin factory at the subpath, no option, no lifecycle hook, and no graph fact, and what the call returns is a bare pack view under [Row views](#row-views). The view measures every row before it writes its first line, which is what buys a column as wide as its widest cell and a fit to the screen, so a sequence rendered through it is buffered whatever its source. It takes one reading of the context's [`columns`](#width-padding-and-multiline-lanes) for the whole render. [ADR-0086](decisions/0086-renders-fit-the-destinations-live-columns-and-tables-shrink-to-fit.md) records the fit.

```ts
// @loomcli/plugins/table
function table<Row>(config?: TableConfig<Row>): View<readonly Row[]>;

interface TableConfig<Row> {
  columns?: readonly Column<Row>[];
}
type Column<Row> = (keyof Row & string) | ColumnEntry<Row>;
type ColumnEntry<Row> = {
  [Key in keyof Row & string]: {
    key: Key;
    header?: string;
    align?: 'left' | 'right' | 'center';
    format?: (value: Row[Key], row: Readonly<Row>, context: ViewContext) => string;
  };
}[keyof Row & string];
```

```ts
import { Command } from '@loomcli/core';
import { table } from '@loomcli/plugins/table';

import { countFiles } from '../actions/count-files.js';

interface Row {
  count: number;
  source: string;
}

export const count = new Command('count')
  .argument('files', { required: true, variadic: true })
  .rows<Row>({
    views: {
      table: table({
        columns: [
          { key: 'count', header: 'COUNT', align: 'right' },
          { key: 'source', header: 'SOURCE' },
        ],
      }),
    },
  })
  .action(countFiles);
```

```text
COUNT  SOURCE
    6  one.txt
    2  two words.txt
    8  total
```

- **Configuration.** `columns` is an ordered list whose entries are a bare key or `{ key, header?, align?, format? }`, where a bare key is `{ key }` and the list order is the column order. A key may appear twice, which is two columns over one field, each with its own header, alignment, and format. With `columns` omitted, every own key that appears in the rows is a column in first-seen order with the key as its header. The configuration is plain data the returned view holds: the factory publishes no fact and no descriptor, and an application that wants another layout names another view.
- **Form.** One header line, then one line per row in source order. A header cell is the entry's `header` or the key spelled as written, styled `dim`. Two spaces separate one column from the next. There are no borders and no rule lines, and the last column of a line carries no padding, so a left- or center-aligned last cell ends its line and a right-aligned one keeps only the padding before it. A row whose cells wrap takes several lines, under **Fit**. Every line ends with `\n`, and the view owns every newline it writes.
- **Cells.** A default cell is `String(value)` passed through `style.escape` and styled `primary`, and `null` and `undefined` print as the empty string rather than as their spellings. A `format` entry replaces the default cell and returns marked text its author owns, which the view neither escapes nor styles, the view-function rule of [Rendered output](#rendered-output); a default cell is escaped by the view because the value is data.
- **Width.** When the table fits, each column is padded with core's `pad` to the widest of its header and every cell in that column, each measured with `context.width`, so a styled cell and a wide character land in the same column as a plain narrow one. A table fits when `columns` is `undefined` or its natural width, the padded columns plus the two-space gaps, is at most `columns`. Alignment is `left` unless the entry names `right` or `center`. A cell is never truncated, whatever the destination reports as its width, and no alignment is inferred from a value's type: a number left-aligns until a column asks for `right`.
- **Tabs.** When `columns` is defined, each tab in a cell or a header, a `format` cell and a styled or `nowrap` one included, expands to spaces with [`expandTabs`](#width-padding-and-multiline-lanes) before the table measures, fits, or wraps it, counted from the start of its own input line within the cell. The spaces count toward the column's natural width and its floor as any space does, so a line shows on screen as wide as the table measured it and holds no tab. Off a terminal a tab stays as written.
- **Fit.** When the natural width exceeds `columns`, the columns shrink by levelling from the top. A column's floor is the widest unit `wrap` keeps whole in any of its cells or its header, measured with `context.width`: a word, with an input line's leading spaces on its first word and its trailing spaces on its last, or a `pad` frame or a `nowrap` frame, within one input line. The floor and `wrap` read the same units, so a column at its floor wraps every unit onto a line that fits. Levelling is stated exactly. Find the largest whole level L at which the sum over columns of max(floor, min(natural, L)), plus the gaps, is at most `columns`. Each column's width is max(floor, min(natural, L)). Any remainder goes one column each, from the left, to the columns at exactly L whose natural width exceeds L. The fitted widths and gaps then total exactly `columns` whenever any column narrowed, and the two-space gap stays and counts toward the fit. Columns of natural widths 40, 20, and 6, with floors of 6 or less, end at 20, 20, and 6 with 46 columns left for cells, at 17, 17, and 6 with 40 left, and at 17, 16, and 6 with 39 left, where L is 16 and the remainder of one goes to the first column.
- **Wrapped cells.** Text in a narrowed column wraps inside the column with [`wrap`'s rules](#width-padding-and-multiline-lanes), so rows grow taller and every value stays complete. A header counts toward its column's natural width and its floor, and it wraps like a cell, styled `dim` on every line. Every line of a wrapped cell keeps its column's alignment, because `pad` aligns per line. A cell's `format` output is what the view measures and wraps. A row is as tall as its tallest cell. Each line of a row ends at its rightmost cell that has text at that height, and that cell carries no padding, by the last column's rule: a left-aligned cell ends the line, a center-aligned one keeps only the spaces before it, and a right-aligned one keeps the padding before it. A shorter cell to the left of that cell adds a blank line padded to its column's width, and the columns after it, with the gaps before them, are left off, so no line ends in a gap or in padding. At 30 columns, a table with a `NAME` column and a `NOTE` column of long text renders as:

  ```text
  NAME   NOTE
  build  compiles every package
         and bundles the
         examples
  check  runs the formatter, the
         linter, and the type
         checker
  ```

- **Records fallback.** When a table with rows cannot fit with every column at its floor, it renders as the [records layout](#records), one block per row and no header line. Each label is the entry's header text, or the key spelled as written, styled `dim` and padded to the widest label. Each value is the cell as the table would render it, a default cell or `format` output with the same styling, wrapped at the width left after the label column and its gap. The fallback's row blocks match the records view's row blocks for the same labels and left-aligned values. The fallback has no tail and highlights no identifier. A right- or center-aligned value aligns within its own widest wrapped line, no value line carries trailing padding, and a blank line inside a value carries no alignment and no indent. A line whose value is empty ends at its label, with no padding or gap after it, and a line whose label and value are both empty is an empty line. A blank line separates one block from the next, with none before the first and none after the last. Overflow happens only where a unit `wrap` keeps whole, or a label, exceeds the space, and the terminal soft-wraps it.
- **Off a terminal.** With `columns` undefined, a pipe or an invocation by name for instance, the output is byte for byte the natural-width output, tabs included. Every cell is one line there, so every line reaches the last column, an empty last cell included. A `format` cell that returns several lines keeps today's bytes there: the layout that treats each line of a cell as a row line applies only when `columns` is defined.
- **Empty.** An empty sequence never takes the records fallback. With no rows, the natural width is the headers' alone. With a `columns` list configured, it prints the header line alone, at the fitted widths, levelled and wrapped like any header row, so a filtered run still reports the shape it searched. When even the header floors exceed `columns`, every column sits at its floor and the line overflows. An empty sequence with no `columns` prints nothing, because no key is known.
- **Typing.** `columns` is typed from `Row`, and each entry's `format` receives `Row[Key]` narrowed from that entry's own literal key. Inside a `views` record, and as the second argument of `out.render` over an array, the row type flows in by contextual typing, so a key that is not a key of `Row` is a compile error on that string. Hoisted into a constant the row type does not flow in, so the factory states it, `table<Row>({…})`, or its cell callbacks go unchecked, the rule [Row views](#row-views) states for every pack view.

### Records

The records list is `@loomcli/plugins/records`. Its factory `records<Row>(config)` takes an identifier and an optional field list and returns a row view, `RowView<Row>`, so a record prints as its source yields it and no row waits on the rows behind it. Like the table it installs nothing and returns a bare pack view. `identifier` is required: it names the key whose value identifies the record, which the view styles apart so an operator scanning a long list finds the record it names. The view takes a fresh reading of the context's [`columns`](#width-padding-and-multiline-lanes) for each row, so a record that arrives after a resize wraps at the new width. [ADR-0086](decisions/0086-renders-fit-the-destinations-live-columns-and-tables-shrink-to-fit.md) records the wrapping.

```ts
// @loomcli/plugins/records
function records<Row>(config: RecordsConfig<Row>): RowView<Row>;

interface RecordsConfig<Row> {
  identifier: keyof Row & string;
  fields?: readonly Field<Row>[];
}
type Field<Row> = (keyof Row & string) | FieldEntry<Row>;
type FieldEntry<Row> = {
  [Key in keyof Row & string]: {
    key: Key;
    format?: (value: Row[Key], row: Readonly<Row>, context: ViewContext) => string;
  };
}[keyof Row & string];
```

```ts
import { Command } from '@loomcli/core';
import { records } from '@loomcli/plugins/records';

import { listMembers } from '../actions/list-members.js';

interface Member {
  key: string;
  kind: string;
}

export const members = new Command('members')
  .rows<Member>({ views: { records: records({ identifier: 'key' }) } })
  .action(listMembers);
```

```text
key   user
kind  object with 3 keys

key   tags
kind  array with 2 items

2 records
```

- **Configuration.** `fields` is an ordered list whose entries are a bare key or `{ key, format? }`, where a bare key is `{ key }` and the list order is the field order. A field carries no `header` and no `align`: the key is the label a records list prints, and the value column is one lane, so neither has a second spelling to choose. With `fields` omitted, every own key that appears in the record is a field in first-seen order. `identifier` names a key of `Row` and adds no line of its own: it selects the value the view highlights among the fields it prints, so a `fields` list that omits the identifier's key prints no line for it and highlights nothing.
- **Form.** One field per block of lines: the key padded left to the key column's width, styled `dim`, then two spaces, then the value. On a terminal a line whose value is empty, one whose first line resolves to no character, ends at its key, with no padding and no gap after it, and a line whose key and value are both empty is an empty line. Off a terminal the key keeps its padding and the gap there, as it always has. One blank line separates one record from the next, with none before the first record and none after the last. There are no rule lines. Every line ends with `\n`, and the view owns every newline it writes.
- **Width.** With `fields` declared, the key column is as wide as the widest key in the list, so every record aligns against the same column. Under the all-keys default the key column is as wide as the widest key of that record alone, because a row view sees one row and cannot measure the rows behind it. Keys are measured with `context.width` and padded with core's `pad`, and a key is never truncated.
- **Wrapping.** This is the records layout: a label column, a two-space gap, a value that wraps, and a blank line between records. The table view renders its rows in the same layout when its columns cannot fit, as [Table](#table) states, so one layout serves both. On a terminal each value's tabs expand to spaces with [`expandTabs`](#width-padding-and-multiline-lanes), counted from the start of each input line of the value, so the key column moves no tab stop and no line holds a tab. Then each value wraps with [`wrap`'s rules](#width-padding-and-multiline-lanes) at `columns` minus the key column's width minus the two-space gap, and every continuation line of a value, authored or wrapped, starts with spaces as wide as the key column and the gap, so the values stay in one column. A blank line inside a value, one that resolves to no character whatever style frames it holds, carries no indent and stays empty. When no column is left for the value, the value is not wrapped. A unit `wrap` keeps whole stays whole. Each row takes its own reading of `columns`: a record printed before a resize keeps its layout, and the next record wraps at the new width. Off a terminal, with `columns` undefined, the output is today's bytes, a value with authored line breaks or tabs included. At 30 columns, a record whose `kind` value is long renders as:

  ```text
  key   tags
  kind  array of 12 strings,
        none empty or longer
        than 40 characters
  ```

- **Cells.** A default value is `String(value)` passed through `style.escape` and styled `primary`, except the identifier's value, which is styled `highlight`. `null` and `undefined` print as the empty string, so the key stands alone on its line, with nothing after it on a terminal, as **Form** states. A `format` entry replaces the default and returns marked text its author owns, which the view neither escapes nor styles, the identifier's field included.
- **Head and tail.** `head` prints nothing, because a records list has no column headings to open with. `tail` prints one blank line and then the summary line `<count> records`, styled `dim`, with its own newline, where `count` is the number of rows `row` was called with. One record reads `1 record`, and an empty sequence prints `0 records` with no blank line before it, because no record printed.
- **Typing.** `identifier` and `fields` are typed from `Row`, and each entry's `format` receives `Row[Key]` narrowed from that entry's own literal key. The contextual-typing rule is the table's: inside a `views` record, and as the second argument of `out.render` over an array, a generator, or an async generator, a key that is not a key of `Row` is a compile error on that string, and hoisted the factory states its row type, `records<Row>({…})`, or its cell callbacks go unchecked.

#### Table and records example coverage

The increment is proven when both examples drop their hand-written views for the two factories. [textstat](../examples/textstat/src/application.ts) declares `rows<Row>` over `{ count: number; source: string }`. Its table view names the `COUNT` and `SOURCE` headers, and its action appends `{ count: total, source: 'total' }` when `--total` was supplied. The `Table` type, `tableView`, and the module that held them are deleted. `--format json` prints an array of rows instead of one object. jsonkit's `paths` declares `views: { list: records({ identifier: 'path' }), table: table({ columns: ['path', 'kind'] }) }`, and `pathList` and `pathTable` are deleted. jsonkit's root declares `rows<Member>` over `{ key: string; kind: string }` with `views: { records: records({ identifier: 'key' }) }`. Its line about the document's kind moves to stderr through `out.info`. A scalar document is an empty sequence whose tail prints `0 records`. The implementation re-pins the golden bytes and the transcripts of the [results](#results-example-coverage), [formatter](#formatter-example-coverage), and [failure](#example-coverage-2) coverage paragraphs against the new views. The `jsonkit --help` page under [The help page](#the-help-page) gains an OPTIONS section with its `--format` row because the root now declares a result.

The acceptance tests cover each factory as the second argument of `out.render` and as an entry of a declared result, a column measured against a wide CJK cell and against a styled cell, a `null` and an `undefined` cell under each factory, one key listed twice as two columns, a `format` cell that returns styled text the view leaves unescaped beside a default cell in the same row that the view escapes, the all-keys default in first-seen order under each factory, an empty sequence under the table with `columns` printing the header line alone and without `columns` printing nothing, an empty sequence under records printing `0 records`, a one-row sequence printing `1 record`, and `tail` receiving the row count under `out.render` and under `out.results` alike. The negative type checks cover a column that names a key the row does not carry, a records field that carries `header`, an `identifier` that names a key the row does not carry, and a `format` whose value parameter is typed as something other than the key's own value type, each inside a `views` record and as the second argument of `out.render`, the records cases over an array, a generator, and an async generator, and a table over a generator rejected because a whole view renders a value. Each case runs under Node and Bun.

#### Table and records fit acceptance

The fit is proven under Node and Bun with a host override of plain numbers for the width, and again under a pty-backed host for the resize cases. The acceptance tests cover:

- **At natural width.** A table whose natural width is less than `columns`, one exactly equal to it, and one under `columns` undefined each print the natural-width bytes.
- **Shrunk.** A table one column wider than `columns` shrinks levelling from the top: the widest column narrows to tie the next widest, and then both narrow together. When the tied columns cannot narrow by a whole column each, the leftover columns go one each to the tied columns from left to right. Cells wrap inside their columns with every value complete, each line of a wrapped cell keeps its column's alignment under `right` and `center`, each line ends at its rightmost cell that has text, which carries no padding, so a middle cell taller than the last ends its extra lines at its own text, with no gap or padding after it, a shorter cell to the left of a cell with text adds a padded blank line, and the two-space gap counts toward the fit. A `format` cell is measured and wrapped by its output.
- **The whole width.** A shrunk table's fitted widths and gaps total exactly `columns`, and with a last cell that fills its column, which a right-aligned last column and a full line of wrapped text give, its widest line equals `columns`. The formula is checked with natural widths 40, 20, and 6: 46 columns left for cells give 20, 20, and 6, 40 give 17, 17, and 6, and 39 give 17, 16, and 6, with the remainder going from the left to the columns at exactly L whose natural width exceeds L.
- **Headers.** A header wider than every cell sets its column's natural width, a header word longer than every cell word sets its floor, and a header wraps like a cell.
- **Floors.** A column's floor is the widest unit `wrap` keeps whole: a word, with an input line's leading spaces on its first word and its trailing spaces on its last, or a `pad` frame or a `nowrap` frame, within one input line. A cell `Ada Lovelace ` whose trailing space would pass its column wraps instead, so every line fits and the next column stays aligned, and a cell `abcd      ` is one unit ten columns wide. A cell in `nowrap` raises its column's floor to the whole cell. Columns held at their floors by a long word stay at the floor while the others narrow.
- **An empty sequence.** An empty sequence with a `columns` list configured prints its header line at the fitted widths, levelled and wrapped like any header row, and never takes the records fallback, however narrow `columns` is. When even the header floors exceed `columns`, every column sits at its floor and the line overflows. With no `columns` list it prints nothing.
- **Records fallback.** A table with rows whose floors do not fit `columns` prints one block per row with the header text, or the key as written, as labels, no header line, wrapped values with their column's styling and `format`, and one blank line between blocks. A right- or center-aligned value aligns within its own widest wrapped line, no value line carries trailing padding, and a blank line inside a value carries no alignment and no indent. A fallback line with an empty header and an empty value is an empty line. Overflow happens only where a unit `wrap` keeps whole, or a label, exceeds the space.
- **The records view.** On a terminal each value wraps at the width left after the padded key column, every continuation line of a value, authored or wrapped, is indented under the value, a blank line inside a styled default value or a plain `format` value carries no indent, a line whose value is `null` ends at its key with no padding or gap, so `{ id: 'one', to: null }` at 40 columns prints `to` alone and a key column three wide leaves no padding after `to`, while a pipe keeps the padding and the gap, and the fallback's row blocks match the records view's row blocks for the same labels and left-aligned values, while the fallback has no tail and highlights no identifier. With no column left for the value, the value stays unwrapped.
- **A resize.** Under a pty-backed host, one run renders a table at 100 columns, the window resizes to 60, and the next render fits 60. A streamed records row after the resize wraps at 60, and the rows before it keep their layout.
- **`COLUMNS`.** `COLUMNS=60` over a real width of 100 narrows a table and a records value to 60, `COLUMNS=150` over 100 changes nothing, `COLUMNS=60` on a terminal that reports no width fits 60, and `COLUMNS=60` on a pipe changes nothing.
- **Tabs.** At 16 columns a table with cells `abcde` and `b\tc d` prints `abcde  b       c` and then `       d`, a records value `b\tc` under the key `first` prints `first  b       c`, and a header holding a tab expands as a cell does, so no line passes 16 columns and none holds a tab. A tab in a styled cell expands inside its style, and a tab in a `nowrap` cell expands while the cell stays whole. Piped, the table and the records value keep the tab.
- **Embedded ANSI.** A `format` cell holding an OSC 8 hyperlink, wrapped at 20 columns beside an `owner` column, closes the link at the end of each line, so the link covers neither the gap nor `drew`, and a cell holding a raw SGR color colors no neighbor. A records value holding either wraps with a continuation indent that carries no link and no color. The views split each wrapped value with `splitLines`.
- **Piped output.** A table and a records view rendered to a pipe, under `app.invoke`, and under an MCP tool call are byte for byte the natural-width output, `COLUMNS` set or not. This holds for a `format` cell that returns several lines, a records value with authored line breaks, and a cell or value holding a tab, because the per-line row layout and tab expansion apply only when `columns` is defined.

### List

The list is `@loomcli/plugins/list`. Its factory `list<Item>(config?)` returns a whole view over the collected items, `View<readonly Item[]>`, so the same value reaches a `views` record under `rows<Item>` and the second argument of `out.render`. Like the table it installs nothing and returns a bare pack view under [Row views](#row-views). It is a whole view because an ordered list right-aligns its numbers against the widest one among its siblings, which a row view cannot know, so a sequence rendered through it is buffered whatever its source. It takes one reading of the context's [`columns`](#width-padding-and-multiline-lanes) for the whole render. [ADR-0088](decisions/0088-pack-views-lay-out-lists-headings-rules-prose-and-boxes.md) records the list.

```ts
// @loomcli/plugins/list
function list<Item>(config?: ListConfig<Item>): View<readonly Item[]>;

interface ListConfig<Item> {
  ordered?: boolean;
  format?: (item: Item, index: number, context: ViewContext) => string;
  children?: (item: Item) => readonly Item[] | undefined;
}
```

```ts
import { Command } from '@loomcli/core';
import { list } from '@loomcli/plugins/list';

import { listServices } from '../actions/list-services.js';

interface Service {
  name: string;
  parts?: readonly Service[];
}

export const services = new Command('services')
  .rows<Service>({
    views: { list: list({ children: (service) => service.parts, format: (service) => service.name }) },
  })
  .action(listServices);
```

```text
● api-gateway
● billing
  ● invoices
  ● refunds
● search
```

- **Configuration.** `ordered` numbers the items, and an omitted or `false` `ordered` gives them bullets. `format` renders one item's text from the item, its index among its siblings counting from 0, and the context. `children` names an item's nested items, and an item whose `children` returns `undefined` or an empty list has none. Every key is optional, so `list()` over `string[]` needs no configuration. The configuration is plain data the returned view holds, under [Row views](#row-views).
- **Form.** One block per item in source order: the marker, one space, then the item's text, then its nested items. A bullet is `glyph.bullet`. An ordered marker is the item's position among its siblings counting from 1 and a `.`, right-aligned with `pad` to the widest marker among those siblings, so ` 9.` right-aligns with `10.`. Markers are `dim`. A nested list starts at its parent's text column, so it indents by the parent's padded marker width and one space, and a nested ordered list counts from 1 again. `ordered` applies at every depth. No blank line separates two items. Every line ends with `\n`, and the view owns every newline it writes.
- **Text.** A default item's text is `String(item)` passed through `style.escape` and styled `primary`, and `null` and `undefined` print as the empty string, the table's cell rule. A `format` result replaces the default and is marked text its author owns, which the view neither escapes nor styles. An item whose text is empty writes its marker alone, with no space after it, and a text that ends in a line break gains no empty line, the rule of [Views over a string](#views-over-a-string).
- **Continuation lines.** Every line of an item's text after its first, authored or wrapped, starts at the item's text column, so it hangs under the text and not under the marker, on a terminal and off one. A blank line inside an item's text, one that resolves to no character, carries no indent and stays empty, the records rule.
- **Wrapping.** On a terminal each item's text expands its tabs with [`expandTabs`](#width-padding-and-multiline-lanes), counted from the start of each input line of the text, then wraps with [`wrap`'s rules](#width-padding-and-multiline-lanes) at `columns` minus its text column, and at 1 when that leaves less, and each line is split with `splitLines`, so a style or a hyperlink never runs into the indent. A unit `wrap` keeps whole stays whole and overflows. Off a terminal, with `columns` undefined, the text is not wrapped and its tabs stay as written. At 30 columns a bulleted item whose text is long renders as:

  ```text
  ● refunds, whose retry policy
    lands with this deploy
  ```

- **Empty.** An empty sequence prints nothing.
- **Typing.** `format` and `children` are typed from `Item`. Inside a `views` record, and as the second argument of `out.render` over an array, the item type flows in, so a callback that reads a member `Item` lacks is a compile error. Hoisted into its own constant, the factory states it, `list<Service>({…})`, or its callbacks go unchecked.

### Views over a string

The heading, the rule, prose, and the box are views over a string: each factory returns `View<string>`, so an action writes `out.render(text, prose())`, and a `result<string>()` names one in its `views` record. A box that frames another view takes that view's data type instead, under [Box](#box). Like the table each installs nothing and returns a bare pack view, and each takes one reading of the context's [`columns`](#width-padding-and-multiline-lanes) per render. [ADR-0088](decisions/0088-pack-views-lay-out-lists-headings-rules-prose-and-boxes.md) records the four.

- **Marked text.** The string is marked text its author owns, as a [lane view](#output-and-failures)'s message is, so a styled word inside it keeps its style and the view does not escape it. Raw data goes through `style.escape` first, the rule of [Rendered output](#rendered-output).
- **Lines.** Each view writes whole lines: every line it writes ends with `\n`, a text that ends in a line break gains no empty line, and the view owns every newline it writes. No view writes a blank line above or below itself, so the spacing between two renders is the action's.
- **Empty.** A text that resolves to no character, the empty string or a style or `nowrap` frame around nothing, renders the empty string, except under the rule, where it draws a bare line.
- **Off a terminal.** With `columns` undefined nothing wraps, tabs stay as written except where a box pads a line, and nothing is cut. Only the rule needs a width there, under [Rule](#rule).

### Heading

The heading is `@loomcli/plugins/heading`. Its factory `heading(config?)` returns `View<string>`, a section heading over its text at one of two levels, as the [help page](#the-help-page) has two, with a form of its own. The heading is wayfinding, not content, so both levels are `dim`, and an underline tells level 1 from level 2.

```ts
// @loomcli/plugins/heading
function heading(config?: HeadingConfig): View<string>;

interface HeadingConfig {
  level?: 1 | 2;
}
```

```ts
import { heading } from '@loomcli/plugins/heading';

await out.render('Deployment summary', heading());
await out.render('Services', heading({ level: 2 }));
```

```text
Deployment summary
──────────────────
Services
```

- **Configuration.** `level` defaults to 1.
- **Form.** The text, styled `dim`, then, at level 1, one line of `glyph.line` as wide as the widest line of the text, measured with `context.width`, also `dim`. Level 2 is the text alone. Neither level indents, and the text keeps its author's styling inside the `dim` frame.
- **Wrapping.** On a terminal the text expands its tabs, wraps at `columns`, and is split with `splitLines`, and the underline matches the widest wrapped line, so it is wider than `columns` only when a unit `wrap` keeps whole is. Off a terminal the text is not wrapped, and the underline matches its widest line as written.

### Rule

The rule is `@loomcli/plugins/rule`. Its factory `rule()` returns `View<string>`, a horizontal line across the destination that carries its text as a label, so `out.render('', rule())` draws a bare line and `out.render('Checks', rule())` a labelled one.

```ts
// @loomcli/plugins/rule
function rule(): View<string>;
```

```ts
import { rule } from '@loomcli/plugins/rule';

await out.render('Checks', rule());
await out.render('', rule());
```

At 60 columns they print:

```text
── Checks ──────────────────────────────────────────────────
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
```

- **Width.** The rule is `columns` wide on a terminal and 80 wide off one. The 80 is the rule's own length, the one view whose form needs a width where none is known, and the context still carries no fallback width under [Width, padding, and multiline lanes](#width-padding-and-multiline-lanes).
- **Bare.** A text that resolves to no character draws `glyph.line` repeated to the rule's width, styled `dim`, and one `\n`.
- **Labelled.** Any other text is the label: two `glyph.line` and a space, `dim`, then the label, its tabs expanded first on a terminal, then a space and `glyph.line` repeated to the rule's width, `dim`. The label keeps its author's styling and adds none. A label too long for one line wraps on a terminal at the rule's width minus five, and at 1 when that leaves less, the three columns before it and at least one space and one line after it, and is split with `splitLines`. Its lines after the first, authored or wrapped, start three spaces in, under the label, a blank line among them, one that resolves to no character, carries no indent and stays empty, the records rule, except the last, which carries the line after it, and only its last line carries the line after it, at least one `glyph.line` long, so the rule overflows only where a unit `wrap` keeps whole does. Off a terminal the label is not wrapped, and an authored line break in it takes the same layout.

### Prose

Prose is `@loomcli/plugins/prose`. Its factory `prose()` returns `View<string>`, paragraphs wrapped to the destination. It is the wrapped counterpart of `print`, which writes its text as it is under [ADR-0086](decisions/0086-renders-fit-the-destinations-live-columns-and-tables-shrink-to-fit.md).

```ts
// @loomcli/plugins/prose
function prose(): View<string>;
```

```ts
import { prose } from '@loomcli/plugins/prose';

await out.render(
  'Three services rolled out to the staging cluster. One health check is still warming up.',
  prose(),
);
```

At 34 columns it prints:

```text
Three services rolled out to the
staging cluster. One health check
is still warming up.
```

- **Form.** The text as its author wrote it, with no styling added. Authored line breaks and blank lines stay, so a blank line separates two paragraphs.
- **Wrapping.** On a terminal the text expands its tabs, wraps at `columns` with [`wrap`'s rules](#width-padding-and-multiline-lanes), and is split with `splitLines`: an input line's leading spaces stay on its first line, and its continuation lines start at column 0. Off a terminal a non-empty text prints as written, with `\n` added when it does not end in a line break.

### Box

The box is `@loomcli/plugins/box`. Its factory `box(config?)` frames text, or the output of another view, in a border with an optional title. With no `content` it returns `View<string>` and frames its text. With `content` it returns a view over the content's data, renders the content inside the frame, and narrows the content's `columns` by the frame, so a table framed in a box shrinks to fit inside it, or falls back to the records layout, under [Table](#table).

```ts
// @loomcli/plugins/box
function box<Data = string>(
  ...config: [Data] extends [string] ? [config?: BoxConfig<Data>] : [config: BoxConfig<Data>]
): View<Data>;

type BoxConfig<Data> = { title?: string } & ([Data] extends [string]
  ? { content?: View<Data> }
  : { content: View<Data> });
```

```ts
import { Command } from '@loomcli/core';
import { box } from '@loomcli/plugins/box';
import { table } from '@loomcli/plugins/table';

import { listPools } from '../actions/list-pools.js';

interface Pool {
  pool: string;
  instances: number;
  status: string;
}

await out.render('All three services passed their health checks.', box({ title: 'Totals' }));

export const pools = new Command('pools')
  .rows<Pool>({ views: { boxed: box({ content: table(), title: 'Pools' }), table: table() } })
  .action(listPools);
```

```text
╭─ Totals ───────────────────────────────────────╮
│ All three services passed their health checks. │
╰────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
╭─ Pools ───────────────────╮
│ pool   instances  status  │
│ blue   4          ready   │
│ green  4          warming │
╰───────────────────────────╯
```

- **Configuration.** `title` is marked text its author owns, as a table's authored `header` is. `content` is a bare view or a declared view's value; inside a box nothing resolves an override for it, because the box calls the view it was given, the rule a bare view follows under `out.render`.
- **Form.** A top border, one line per content line, and a bottom border, every border piece `dim`. The top border is `glyph.lineDownRightArc`, then `glyph.line` across, then `glyph.lineDownLeftArc`, and with a title it reads `glyph.lineDownRightArc`, `glyph.line`, a space, the title styled `primary` and `bold`, a space, then `glyph.line` to the corner. A content line is `glyph.lineVertical` and a space, the line padded with `pad` to the inner width, then a space and `glyph.lineVertical`. The bottom border is `glyph.lineUpRightArc`, `glyph.line` across, and `glyph.lineUpLeftArc`. The inner width is the widest content line, measured with `context.width`, or the title's width and two when that is wider, so the title always sits in the top border with at least one `glyph.line` after it.
- **Text content.** With no `content` the box frames its text. On a terminal the text expands its tabs, wraps at `columns` minus 4, and at 1 when that leaves less, and is split with `splitLines`, so the box is as wide as its text and never wider than `columns` unless a unit `wrap` keeps whole, or the title, is. Off a terminal the text is not wrapped, and the box is as wide as its widest line.
- **View content.** With `content` the box calls the content's view function with its data and a context that matches its own except for `columns`, which is `columns` minus 4, and 1 when that leaves less, on a terminal and stays `undefined` off one. The content's text is split with `splitLines`, so its trailing newline adds no line, and on a terminal its tabs expand before the box measures it. A content line wider than the space the box offers, which a content view that ignores `columns` writes, widens the box past `columns`, and nothing is cut.
- **Tabs.** Off a terminal a tab in a content line expands inside the line's `pad` frame, counted from the line's start, so the right border stays in its column.
- **Empty.** A text box over a text that resolves to no character, and a box whose content renders such a text, print nothing.
- **Typing.** `Data` is inferred from `content`, or from the context the box is written in, and is `string` when neither supplies it. Only a box whose `Data` is a string may leave out its configuration or its `content`. Inside a `views` record the record's data type flows through the box into the content's factory, so `box({ content: table({ columns: ['nope'] }) })` under `rows<Pool>` is a compile error on `'nope'`, and a box with no `content` under a result whose value is not a string is a compile error: `box()` misses its required configuration, and `box({ title })` names the missing `content`. Hoisted, the content's factory states its type, `box({ content: table<Pool>() })`.

#### List, heading, rule, prose, and box example coverage

The increment is proven when jsonkit's `doctor` Command, which the private `@loom/doctor` plugin attaches, reports its checks through the pack views in place of its one `print` line. Its action renders `Host checks` through `heading()`, then a `list<string>()` of two checks, `Platform: <host.platform>` and `Output: a terminal` or `Output: not a terminal` from `host.terminal.stdout.isTTY`, then `''` through `rule()`, then `All checks passed.` through `box({ title: 'Result' })`. `@loom/doctor` depends on `@loomcli/plugins`, and the [plugin Commands](#plugin-commands) example and `jsonkit doctor`'s transcripts re-pin against the new output. Piped, it prints:

```text
Host checks
───────────
● Platform: linux
● Output: not a terminal
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
╭─ Result ───────────╮
│ All checks passed. │
╰────────────────────╯
```

#### List, heading, rule, prose, and box acceptance

Each case runs under Node and Bun, at a fixed width through a host override of plain numbers and with `columns` undefined, and checks exact bytes. The acceptance tests cover:

- **Each factory twice.** Each view as the second argument of `out.render`, and the list and the text views as entries of a declared result under `rows<Item>` and `result<string>()`.
- **The list.** Bullets and ordered markers, ordered markers right-aligned from ` 9.` to `10.`, `null` and `undefined` items printing empty, a default item escaped beside a `format` item left unescaped, `format` receiving each item's index among its siblings, two levels of `children` with each level starting at its parent's text column and a nested ordered list counting from 1, a wrapped item hanging under its text at 30 columns, an authored line break hanging under its text piped, a blank line inside an item carrying no indent, a tab expanding on a terminal and kept piped, and an empty sequence printing nothing.
- **The heading.** Level 1 and level 2, a level 1 underline as wide as a CJK text and as a styled text, a wrapped level 1 underline matching its widest wrapped line, and a word wider than `columns` keeping its line and widening its underline.
- **The rule.** A bare and a labelled rule at 60 columns and piped at 80, a label wrapped at a narrow width with its continuation lines under the label and the line on its last line alone, a blank label line printing empty and a blank last label line carrying the line after it, and a label word too wide to fit overflowing with one `glyph.line` after it.
- **Prose.** Paragraphs separated by a blank line, a leading indent kept on the first line, a tab expanding on a terminal and kept piped, a text with and without a trailing line break, and an OSC 8 hyperlink closing at each wrapped line's end.
- **The box.** A text box with and without a title, a title wider than its text setting the inner width, text wrapped at `columns` minus 4, a table framed at a width where it shrinks and at one where it falls back to records, a content view that ignores `columns` widening the box, a declared view's override not applying inside a box, a tab in piped content keeping the right border in its column, and the empty string printing nothing.
- **Empty text.** Under each view over a string, the empty string, a style frame around nothing such as `style.dim('')`, and a `nowrap` frame around nothing each render the empty string, on a terminal and piped, except that the rule draws its bare line, a box with a title over such a text prints nothing, and a box whose `content` view renders such a text prints nothing, titled and untitled.
- **A resize.** Under a pty-backed host, one run renders a rule and a box at 100 columns, the window resizes to 60, and the next rule and box fit 60.
- **Typing.** The negative type checks cover a list `format` whose item parameter is not `Item`, a `children` that returns another type, a heading `level` of 3, a box with no `content` under `result<Summary>()`, and a column the row does not carry inside a boxed table.

### Loom theme

```ts
import type { AdaptiveStyle, ConcreteStyle, Plugin, ThemeConstraint, ThemeMapping } from '@loomcli/core';

type LoomThemeDefaults = Readonly<
	{ primary: ConcreteStyle } & Record<
		'dim' | 'highlight' | 'success' | 'warning' | 'error' | 'info',
		AdaptiveStyle // new: the six colored tokens adapt to the run's background
	>
>;

export type LoomThemeOverrides = {
	readonly [Name in keyof LoomThemeDefaults]?: ConcreteStyle | AdaptiveStyle | undefined; // AdaptiveStyle is new
} & ThemeMapping;

export declare function loomTheme<const Mapping extends ThemeMapping = {}>(
	overrides?: LoomThemeOverrides & Mapping & ThemeConstraint<Mapping>,
): Plugin<{}, LoomThemeDefaults & Omit<NoInfer<Mapping>, keyof LoomThemeDefaults>>;
```

```ts
import { Application, style } from '@loomcli/core';
import { loomTheme } from '@loomcli/plugins/theme';

const app = new Application('example', {
	plugins: [loomTheme({
		highlight: style.cyan.bold,
		identifier: style.hex('#C97B36', { ansi256: 172, ansi16: 'yellow' }),
	})],
});
```

- **Status.** Implemented under ADR-0022 and [ADR-0029](decisions/0029-explicit-color-fallbacks-preserve-theme-hues.md). The adaptive tokens and their light side are proposed under [ADR-0092](decisions/0092-core-settles-each-runs-background-once-and-a-theme-entry-may-adapt-to-it.md).
- **Exports.** `@loomcli/plugins/theme` adds `loomTheme` and the type `LoomThemeOverrides` beside the existing `theme(mapping)`. Both factories use identity `@loomcli/plugins/theme` and contribute through the same single theme slot. They install no middleware, options, hooks, or views. Importing either factory installs nothing.
- **Defaults.** `loomTheme()` supplies the seven mappings below. `primary` is a plain entry, and the six colored tokens are [adaptive](#background), with a dark side and a light side, so core resolves each to the side that matches the run's background. `theme(mapping)` remains the bare factory and supplies only its declared mappings. The named defaults change foregrounds only, preserving backgrounds and modifiers. The factory takes no mode argument and reads no environment variable: core settles the background under [Background](#background), and the operator's spelling comes from the [background plugin](#background-plugin).
- **Overrides.** A supplied concrete chain replaces the complete mapping for its key, both sides and every fallback color, so a plain override is one value on both backgrounds. An adaptive override supplies both sides. An omitted or `undefined` built-in override retains the default. `style` contributes no operations and inherits its surroundings. `style.resetForeground` selects the terminal's foreground default while preserving other attributes. `null` and applied strings are invalid values. The existing concrete-chain and reserved-name rules apply.
- **Custom names.** Extra keys add tokens to the Application vocabulary, including keys whose value is `undefined`. Core-key completion suggests the seven names without requiring an annotation. A reusable mapping can use `satisfies LoomThemeOverrides` while retaining its custom keys. Literal custom names survive the returned plugin and [Application environment registration](#theme-plugins-and-typed-names) into action and view contexts. The imported `style` remains independent of Application registration. A mapping cannot reference another token.
- **Policy.** Construction reads no terminal facts. Core selects colors for each destination under the existing rendering policy. Installing the theme does not force color, select glyph forms, or change layout. An ordinary pipe remains free of styling, while explicit policy or `FORCE_COLOR` can enable it. Under automatic policy, `NO_COLOR` suppresses colors unless `FORCE_COLOR` is also set. Authored modifiers follow their own policy. Theme installation leaves unmarked text unchanged.

The named palette uses [explicit fallback colors](#explicit-color-fallbacks) at the reduced depths. On a dark background, and when the run's background is `undefined`:

| Token | Truecolor foreground | 256-color foreground | 16-color foreground |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `primary` | Terminal default | Terminal default | Terminal default |
| `dim` | `#8B93A3` | `245` | `brightBlack` |
| `highlight` | `#C97B36` | `172` | `yellow` |
| `success` | `#7A8F7B` | `108` | `green` |
| `warning` | `#E2B93D` | `178` | `brightYellow` |
| `error` | `#C04532` | `131` | `red` |
| `info` | `#5B7DA3` | `67` | `blue` |

On a light background:

| Token | Truecolor foreground | 256-color foreground | 16-color foreground |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `primary` | Terminal default | Terminal default | Terminal default |
| `dim` | `#5F6B7A` | `243` | `brightBlack` |
| `highlight` | `#9C5A1E` | `130` | `yellow` |
| `success` | `#4E6B50` | `65` | `green` |
| `warning` | `#8A6D0E` | `94` | `brightYellow` |
| `error` | `#C04532` | `131` | `red` |
| `info` | `#4A6B91` | `60` | `blue` |

Each light truecolor value holds a contrast of at least 4.5:1 on a cream background. The 16-color fallbacks keep the dark side's names, because a light terminal remaps its own sixteen colors for its background. `error` holds the same values on both sides. `primary` maps to `style.resetForeground`, not a fixed white or cream, so it follows the terminal on either background. `dim` uses a color, not `faint`. No default adds bold. A view requests emphasis through a chain such as `style.highlight.bold(text)`. The palette paints no background; its colored tokens adapt to the run's.

#### Loom theme acceptance

The implementation increment proves these cases through public APIs:

- Packed consumers import both factories and `LoomThemeOverrides` from the same subpath. Neither import installs a plugin. Installing either with another theme fails the existing identity or theme-slot check.
- Every default emits the exact foreground in the dark table at each depth under a dark background, and in the light table under a light one, with no background or modifier operation. A nested `primary` restores terminal foreground inside a colored span while preserving the surrounding background and modifiers.
- Omitted and `undefined` overrides retain defaults. A replacement chain discards the original mapping, both of its sides, and their fallbacks, and emits the same bytes under both backgrounds; an adaptive replacement emits its own sides. `style` inherits the enclosing style, and `style.resetForeground` restores terminal foreground. Custom `undefined` keys remain valid tokens.
- Compiler checks cover literal custom names, an adaptive override and an adaptive custom key, independent imported styles, invalid values, reserved names, and semantic references. An editor completion check suggests all seven core keys and omits keys already supplied.
- Both examples install `loomTheme()`. `textstat --total` uses the default highlight for its total row on a color terminal. Under ordinary piping or automatic `NO_COLOR`, the same content and layout contain no color escapes. Help and version restyling remains a separate increment.
- Process fixtures run on Node and Bun against the built packages. Packed-consumer evidence exercises the published declarations and the named palette at each color depth.

`scripts/check-theme-contract.mjs` checks the built factory export against the compiler and editor. `check:types` runs it after the existing declaration checks, so `pnpm verify` and PR CI include it. It verifies compilation and editor completion, not palette merging or output behavior. For a standalone run, use `pnpm build && node scripts/check-theme-contract.mjs`.

### Manifest

```ts
// @loomcli/plugins/manifest
import type { BooleanOption, Plugin, PluginOptions, ResultNode } from '@loomcli/core';

const options = {
  manifest: { control: true, description: "Print this command's manifest as JSON.", type: 'boolean' },
} satisfies PluginOptions;
export type ManifestOptions = typeof options;
export interface ManifestSettings {
  readonly short?: NonNullable<BooleanOption['short']>;
}
export declare function manifest(settings?: ManifestSettings): Plugin<ManifestOptions>;

// The document the option prints, as JSON. The package exports no type for it.
interface ManifestDocument {
  readonly name: string;
  readonly version: string;
  readonly description: string | null;
  readonly tokens: string;
  readonly exitCodes: Readonly<Record<string, string>>; // core's five rows and a row per declared code, in ascending numeric order
  readonly encodings: { readonly json: string; readonly jsonl: string };
  readonly globals: readonly ManifestOption[];
  readonly command: ManifestCommand;
}
interface ManifestCommand {
  readonly name: string | null;
  readonly path: readonly string[];
  readonly description: string | null;
  readonly details: readonly string[];
  readonly examples: readonly { readonly command: string; readonly note: string | null }[];
  readonly deprecated: string | null;
  readonly hasAction: boolean;
  readonly result: ResultNode | null;
  readonly failures: readonly ManifestFailure[];
  readonly arguments: readonly ManifestArgument[];
  readonly options: readonly ManifestOption[];
  readonly children: readonly ManifestCommand[];
}
interface ManifestFailure {
  readonly code: string; // the class's failure code, in place of the retired hand-written name
  readonly exitCode: number;
  readonly meaning: string;
}
interface ManifestArgument {
  readonly name: string;
  readonly description: string | null;
  readonly required: boolean;
  readonly variadic: boolean;
  readonly schema: Readonly<Record<string, unknown>> | null;
  readonly default: { readonly value: unknown } | null;
}
type ManifestOption =
  | {
      readonly type: 'string';
      readonly name: string;
      readonly description: string | null;
      readonly deprecated: string | null;
      readonly control: boolean; // new: see Control options
      readonly long: string | null;
      readonly short: string | null;
      readonly required: boolean;
      readonly requiredWhen: 'non-interactive' | null; // new: see Interaction
      readonly multiple: boolean;
      readonly schema: Readonly<Record<string, unknown>> | null;
      readonly env: readonly string[];
      readonly default: { readonly value: unknown } | null;
      readonly implied: string | null;
      readonly background: boolean; // new: see Background
    }
  | {
      readonly type: 'boolean';
      readonly name: string;
      readonly description: string | null;
      readonly deprecated: string | null;
      readonly control: boolean;
      readonly long: string | null;
      readonly short: string | null;
      readonly negative: string | null;
      readonly polarity: 'positive' | 'negative' | 'both';
      readonly interaction: boolean; // new: see Interaction
      readonly color: boolean; // new: see Color
      readonly schema: Readonly<Record<string, unknown>> | null;
      readonly env: readonly string[];
    }
  | {
      readonly type: 'count';
      readonly name: string;
      readonly description: string | null;
      readonly deprecated: string | null;
      readonly control: boolean;
      readonly long: string | null;
      readonly short: string | null;
      readonly verbose: boolean; // new: see Verbosity
      readonly quiet: boolean; // new: see Verbosity
      readonly schema: null;
      readonly env: readonly string[];
    };
```

`jsonkit get --manifest` prints the document below, abridged here to its first global; the full `globals` list continues with `--help`, `--version`, `--manifest`, `--explain`, `--color`, `--verbose`, and `--quiet`.

```json

  "version": "0.0.0",
```
