- **Implied values.** In a fixture with `backup` implying `simple` and a closed set of values, `--backup=<Tab>` offers the values as whole words that begin `--backup=`, and `--backup <Tab>` offers what the next word may be and no value.
- **Values.** `jsonkit paths --format <Tab>` and `--format=<Tab>` offer the view names, the second as whole words that begin `--format=`, `jsonkit get --file <Tab>` falls back to file names, and `jsonkit paths --format a<Tab>`, which matches no view, offers no file name either.
- **Injection.** In a fixture application, a closed-set value `$(touch sentinel)`, one holding a backtick command, and one holding `;touch sentinel` are each inserted as text, two values that share the prefix `$(touch sentinel)` or `a b` insert that prefix as quoted text, values holding `\` and `\:` insert as they are, a value holding a newline is not offered, a typed word `$(touch sentinel)` before the cursor is passed as text, in Bash a typed `$((x[$(touch sentinel)]))/` or `$HOME/` under the file fallback runs and rewrites nothing, and no sentinel file ever exists. A unit test shows that each script generator refuses a name outside the portable set and that the script printed for each portable name sources without running anything.
- **Failing closed.** An unknown command earlier in the line, an unclosed quote under the cursor, a callback that exits nonzero, and an answer whose directive line is a bare `:` each offer nothing.
- **Framing.** A unit test reads `__complete` answers for every position kind, descriptions with tabs and line breaks, and directive lines, byte for byte.
- **PowerShell.** A real `pwsh` on Linux and macOS, under Node and Bun, dot-sources the script `jsonkit completion powershell` prints and answers through `TabExpansion2`, the function PowerShell's Tab calls, the Commands, Options, and Values cases above, and the Injection cases with a typed `$(New-Item sentinel)` and an offered value holding it, with no sentinel file ever existing. An offered value holding `’` is inserted single-quoted with the `’` doubled, and a program that resolves to a `.cmd` file is never called. A unit test reads the startup line and the quoted script path for a path holding `'` and each of U+2018 through U+201B. Windows PowerShell is unverified.
- **Installing.** Process tests under Node and Bun set `HOME`, `XDG_DATA_HOME`, `XDG_CONFIG_HOME`, `XDG_STATE_HOME`, and the working directory to temporary directories and clear `ZDOTDIR`, `SHELL`, and `PSModulePath` unless a case sets them:
  - `install bash` and `install zsh` write the pinned script files with mode `644` under umask `002` and `077`, add the pinned startup line at the end of the pinned startup file, creating it when it is missing and adding a line break first when it does not end with one, record both in `completion.<shell>.json`, and print the pinned lines. A second install prints the unchanged and already-loads lines and changes no byte. `install fish` writes `<config>/fish/completions/jsonkit.fish`, records it, touches no startup file, and prints the unchanged line on a second install. `install` with no shell follows `SHELL`, `/usr/bin/zsh` selecting `zsh`, and an unknown or unset `SHELL` exits 2 with the pinned sentence. On `darwin`, Bash's line goes to an existing `.profile` when neither `.bash_profile` nor `.bash_login` exists. An absolute `ZDOTDIR` moves the Zsh line under it, including to a folder that does not exist yet, which install creates. After `XDG_DATA_HOME` changes, a second install writes the script at the new path, removes the recorded one, and replaces its line where it stands, printing `Updated the line in <startup>.`
  - A real interactive Bash, Zsh, and Fish, driven through a pseudo-terminal with the temporary home and its startup files, complete `jsonkit <Tab>` after `install` alone, Bash run as a login shell on `darwin` and as an interactive shell elsewhere. Zsh completes with a `.zshrc` that never runs `compinit`, with one that runs it before the line, with one that runs it again after the line, with one whose only `compinit` runs after the line, on a second shell start, and with an insecure folder on `fpath`, never asking a question; under umask `002`, a `compinit` after the line never asks either. Applications named `files` and `describe` complete their Commands, and Zsh's own file completion still works after them. A real `pwsh` whose profile `install pwsh` wrote completes through `TabExpansion2` after it loads that profile.
  - An unrecorded file at a script's path, and a recorded script changed since, each fail `install` and `update` with exit 1, print the refused line, and change no byte of the script or the startup file. With Bash and Zsh installed and the Zsh script edited, `update` fails and changes no byte of either shell. A startup file that is a directory fails with the pinned sentence and writes nothing. A startup file the process may not write, one in a folder it may not write, one owned by another user, and one in UTF-16BE each install the script, print the line to add, record no line, and exit 0. After a recorded startup file gains bytes that are not UTF-8, `install` and `update` keep its line recorded and print nothing for it, and `uninstall` prints the line to remove. With Bash and Zsh installed and Bash's plugin's file damaged, `uninstall` with no shell fails and changes no byte of either shell. After a startup file becomes one the process may not write, `uninstall` removes the script, prints the line to remove, deletes the plugin's file, and exits 0, and a second `uninstall` prints the nothing-to-remove line.
  - After the fixture's script changes, `update` rewrites each recorded script at its recorded path, even with `XDG_DATA_HOME` changed since, and prints the updated lines, and after the line's text changes, it replaces the line where it stands. After the operator removed the line, `update` adds none. After the line's text changes and the startup file becomes one the process may not write, `update` rewrites the script, prints the line to remove and the line to add in its place, records no line, and exits 0. With a `.zshrc` the process may not write and then an absolute `ZDOTDIR` set, `install` adds the new line under `ZDOTDIR`, prints the old line to remove, and exits 0. With nothing recorded, `update` and `uninstall` print their nothing-to lines and exit 0. After a first install killed before its script was written, `update` prints the nothing-to-update line and leaves the pending file, which the next `install` recovers.
  - `uninstall` removes the script, the line, and each created directory then empty, deletes the plugin's file, and leaves a startup file that ended with a line break before `install` byte for byte as it was. A startup line the operator edited stays and prints the left-as-it-is line, and a script the operator edited stays and prints the left-in-place line. `uninstall` with no shell removes every installed shell, and `uninstall zsh` leaves Bash's script and line.
  - `install pwsh` against a fixture `pwsh` on `PATH` that answers a Base64 profile path holding non-ASCII characters and `RemoteSigned` writes the line there. Fixtures that cannot start, exit 1, or answer a relative path each fail with the pinned sentence and write nothing, and ones that answer `Restricted` and `AllSigned` each install the script, print the policy sentence and the line, record no line, and exit 0. After the policy changes to `Restricted`, `uninstall` runs no shell and removes the line. A fixture `pwsh` in the working directory and one under a relative `PATH` entry are never run. On a `win32` fixture host with `SHELL` unset, `PSModulePath` holding `C:\Users\me\Documents\PowerShell\Modules`, as every PowerShell 7 adds, including one from the Microsoft Store, selects `pwsh`, and one holding only `WindowsPowerShell` folders selects `powershell`.
- **Refreshing.** `refreshCompletion`, given a fixture binary path, runs it with `completion update`, pipes its output into the host's streams, and resolves; a child that exits 1, and a path that cannot start, each add the pinned `warn` log event and resolve. Installed as `selfUpdate({ afterReplace: refreshCompletion })` under the self-update fixture, an update rewrites a recorded script to the replaced binary's version.
- **Packed consumers.** A consumer installs the packed pack, imports `@loomcli/plugins/completion`, compiles against its declaration, and prints a script.

### Man pages

```ts
// @loomcli/plugins/manpage
import type { Host, Log, Plugin } from '@loomcli/core';

export interface RefreshContext {
  readonly path: string; // the binary that replaced this one
  readonly host: Host; // the run's host
  readonly signal: AbortSignal; // the run signal
  readonly log: Log; // the run's log
}
export declare function manpage(): Plugin;
export declare function refreshManpages(context: RefreshContext): Promise<void>;
```

```ts
import { Application } from '@loomcli/core';
import { help } from '@loomcli/plugins/help';
import { manpage, refreshManpages } from '@loomcli/plugins/manpage';
import { selfUpdate } from '@loomcli/plugins/self-update';

export const jsonkit = new Application('jsonkit', {
  plugins: [help(), manpage(), selfUpdate({ afterReplace: refreshManpages })],
});
```

```text
$ jsonkit manpage install
Installed 20 man pages in /home/me/.local/share/man/man1.
Read them with man jsonkit.
$ man -w jsonkit-get
/home/me/.local/share/man/man1/jsonkit-get.1
$ jsonkit manpage uninstall
Removed 20 man pages from /home/me/.local/share/man/man1.
$ jsonkit manpage generate --out build/man
Wrote 20 man pages to /home/me/src/jsonkit/build/man.
```

`manpage()` is the manpage plugin. It writes one [man page](glossary.md#product-surface) for each Command an operator can find, in the roff that `man` reads, from the graph and the help facts each Command carries, and installs, refreshes, and removes the set in the operator's home folder. Its identity is `@loomcli/plugins/manpage`, and it declares no settings, no options, no middleware, and no extension; it contributes one [plugin Command](#plugin-commands) group and one `onGraphBuilt` hook. [ADR-0079](decisions/0079-the-manpage-plugin-writes-a-roff-page-per-command-and-installs-the-set-in-the-home-folder.md) records the decision.

- **The Commands.** `manpage` is a group, `Write or install the man pages.`, with these children:
  - `generate`, `Write the man pages to a folder.`, with one required string option, `--out`, `The folder to write the man pages in. It is created when missing.`, whose help placeholder is `folder`.
  - `install`, `Install the man pages in your home folder.`, with no argument or option.
  - `update`, `Bring installed man pages up to date with this version.`, with no argument or option.
  - `uninstall`, `Remove the installed man pages.`, with no argument or option.

  No child declares a result, so `--format` never applies, and every child writes through `out`.
- **What it reads.** A page reads the `CommandNode` it describes, its parent and visible children, `graph.name`, `graph.version`, `graph.globals` on the root page, and the extension values those nodes carry under `helpCommand`, `helpInput`, and `helpArgument` from `@loomcli/plugins/help/extension` and `configInput` from `@loomcli/plugins/config/extension`, through `readExtension`, as a projection reads any plugin's facts. Neither plugin need be installed: a value is read wherever a node carries it, and a page without help's values is shorter, with no details and no EXAMPLES. A page reads no host fact, so the same graph gives the same bytes on every host, from every build, and through `generate` and `install` alike.
- **Which applications.** A root that declares arguments cannot hold children, so textstat cannot install the plugin, as [Plugin Commands](#plugin-commands) states, and an application installs it once, because a second `manpage` collides there.

#### The page set

- **One page per findable Command.** The set holds one page for the root and one for every Command that is not hidden and has no hidden ancestor, plugin Commands and groups included, so `jsonkit-manpage-install` has a page and the completion plugin's hidden `__complete` has none. A deprecated Command has a page. An alias has no page and appears on none.
- **Names.** A page's name is the application name, then each name on the Command's path, joined with `-`: `jsonkit` for the root, `jsonkit-get`, and `jsonkit-completion-install`. Its file is the name and `.1`, because every page is in section 1.
- **Names that collide.** Two pages whose names are equal when ASCII letters are compared without case would be one file on a file system that ignores case, such as macOS's default. The plugin's `onGraphBuilt` hook judges the page names on every build and throws a `DeclarationError` under the rule `@loomcli/plugins/manpage/page-name-taken`, which reports as itself under [Judging the built graph](#judging-the-built-graph): `Commands "foo-bar" and "foo bar" both give the man page jsonkit-foo-bar. Rename one of them, or hide one.` When the two names differ in case, the sentence names both, `Commands "Get" and "get" give the man pages jsonkit-Get and jsonkit-get, which one file holds on a file system that ignores case. Rename one of them, or hide one.` A hidden Command gives no page, so it collides with nothing.

#### The page

A page is roff for the `man` macro package, read by man-db's `groff` and by `mandoc`, the `man` of macOS and the BSDs. It is ASCII, each line ends with a line feed, the last line included, and no line ends in whitespace. It holds no blank line, an empty line of code being written `\&`, no comment, and no date. With jsonkit's `get` details in `get.md` under [Markdown details](#markdown-details), `jsonkit-get.1` holds this text:

```roff
.TH "JSONKIT\-GET" "1" "" "jsonkit 0.12.0" ""
.SH "NAME"
jsonkit\-get \- Read one value at a path.
.SH "SYNOPSIS"
.nf
\fBjsonkit get\fR <path> [options]
.fi
.SH "DESCRIPTION"
A path is a dot\-separated walk from the root of the document.
.IP \(bu 2
A \fBkey\fR reads an object\(aqs member, such as \fBuser.name\fR.
.IP \(bu 2
A \fBwhole number\fR reads an array\(aqs item, such as \fBitems.0\fR.
.PP
The document is \fIJSON\fR; see the format <https://www.json.org/json\-en.html>.
.SH "ARGUMENTS"
.TP
\fIpath\fR
Dot path to read.
.SH "EXAMPLES"
.nf
\fB$ jsonkit get name \-f doc.json\fR
.fi
.PP
.nf
\fB$ jsonkit get nested.deep.value \-f doc.json\fR
.fi
.SH "SEE ALSO"
\fBjsonkit\fR(1)
```

A page holds these sections, in this order, each omitted when it has nothing to show. `<path>` is the application name followed by the Command's path, space-separated, as on the [help page](#the-help-page).

1. **Title.** `.TH "<NAME>" "1" "" "<name> <version>" ""`: the page name with its ASCII letters in uppercase, the section, an empty date, the application name and `graph.version`, and an empty manual name. The version tells a reader which build wrote the page, and no clock reaches a page.
2. **NAME.** `<page> \- <description>`, or the page name alone when the Command has no description.
3. **SYNOPSIS.** Each usage form help's USAGE block prints for the Command, in its order, one line each in no-fill text, with `<path>` in bold and the rest as help prints it.
4. **DESCRIPTION.** For a deprecated Command, a paragraph `Deprecated: <message>`. Then the Command's `details`, rendered under Markdown below. A Command with neither has no DESCRIPTION.
5. **COMMANDS.** For a Command with a visible child, one entry per visible child, in help's sections and order. An entry's tag is the child's name in bold, followed by help's ` <command>` or ` [command]` suffix, and its text is help's right cell for the row, with `deprecated` as its one possible fact.
6. **ARGUMENTS.** One entry per argument in declaration order. The tag is the name in italic, and the text is help's right cell for the row.
7. **OPTIONS** and **GLOBAL OPTIONS.** The Command's visible local options, in help's sections and order. On the root page, the visible globals take their places in help's option sections, under GLOBAL OPTIONS unless an authored section holds them. The root always has a visible child, the `manpage` group, so help's folding of the globals into OPTIONS on a childless root never applies. On every other page the globals appear nowhere, and SEE ALSO names the root page, which lists them. An entry's tag is help's left cell as help prints it, without its leading indentation, so it reads `-f, --file <path>`, `--[no-]total`, `-v, --verbose...`, or `-b, --backup[=<control>]`. Each spelling, the bracketed `[no-]` included, is bold, each placeholder between `<` and `>` is italic, and the separators, the brackets, the `=`, and the `...` are regular, so `\fB\-f\fR, \fB\-\-file\fR <\fIpath\fR>` and `\fB\-b\fR, \fB\-\-backup\fR[=<\fIcontrol\fR>]`. Its text is help's right cell for the row, the description, the [accepted values](#accepted-values) sentence under help's bound, and the parenthesis of facts. Then, on a line of its own, `Environment: <VARIABLE>` when the option has an [environment binding](#input-sources), naming every variable of a list in declaration order, separated by commas, and on another, `Configuration: <path>` when it carries `configInput`, each value in bold.
8. **EXAMPLES.** For each of the Command's `examples`, a paragraph holding `$ <name> <command>` in bold as one no-fill line, then its note, when it has one, as `.RS 4`, the note's text, and `.RE`, with no `.PP`, so the note sits under its command.
9. **ENVIRONMENT.** One entry per variable of each option the page lists that has an environment binding, in the order the page lists them and, within a list, in declaration order. The tag is the variable in bold, and the text is `Supplies <spelling>.`, with the long spelling of the option's tag in bold, as the tag prints it and without `...`: `--file`, `--no-total` for a negative Boolean, `--[no-]total` for one of both polarities, `--verbose` for a counted option, or the short spelling, `-m`, for a `shortOnly` option.
10. **SEE ALSO.** The root page, the parent's page when the parent is not the root, then each visible child's page in the COMMANDS order, as `\fB<page>\fR(1)` separated by `, `. The root page names its children alone.

- **Sections help orders.** When a Command's members carry [ordered help sections](#ordered-help-sections), the page follows help's grouping and order: an outer heading is a `.SH` and an inner heading an `.SS`, each as help prints it, in uppercase, and the default headings are COMMANDS, OPTIONS, and GLOBAL OPTIONS, as on help. A global member of an authored section appears on the root page alone.
- **One line.** A description, a deprecated message, and a stdin input's description print on one line wherever the page shows them: each line break the author wrote, CRLF or a single terminator, reads as one space, as on the help page.
- **Entries.** Each entry is `.TP`, its tag on the next line, and its text on the line after, a filled paragraph; an extra line, such as `Environment:`, follows a `.br`. An entry whose text is empty, as for a member with no description, no accepted values, and no fact, writes its `.TP` and tag alone, and one with an extra line and no text writes the extra line without the `.br`.
- **Paragraph breaks.** A `.PP` separates a paragraph, a code block, a quote, a thematic break, an example, or an item's later blocks from the block before it; a list item and a heading at the top level of `details` write none, because `.IP` and `.SS` space themselves, while a heading inside a list item or a quote, which prints as a paragraph in bold, takes its `.PP` as any paragraph does. The first block after a `.SH` or `.SS`, or inside an `.RS`, writes none, so no paragraph request follows a heading or opens an indented block. A block that opens an `.RS`, code, a quote, or an item's later blocks, writes its `.PP` before the `.RS` when a block precedes it, so it keeps its space from the text above. An example's note writes none, under EXAMPLES.

#### Roff text

Every string a page prints, an authored fact or a graph fact, passes through one writer:

- **Escapes.** Each `\` is written `\e` and each `-` is written `\-`, so a spelling copied from the page is the one the operator types and no hyphen becomes a typographic one. Each `'` is written `\(aq`, each `` ` `` `\(ga`, each `^` `\(ha`, and each `~` `\(ti`, which groff would otherwise print as typographic quotes and accents where its man.local does not map them back, and each `"` is written `\(dq`, so a quote is never read as roff's argument quoting. A text line that would start with `.` starts with `\&`, so no authored text reads as a request.
- **Request arguments.** Each argument of `.TH`, and the text of each `.SH` and `.SS`, is written as one argument in double quotes, so a heading of several words, or one holding a quote, is read whole.
- **Characters.** A tab in no-fill text, a code line or an example, is kept, and `man` moves it to the next tab stop; a tab anywhere else is written as a space. Every other control character, U+0000 through U+001F or U+007F through U+009F, and each line separator, U+2028 or U+2029, is written as [`escapeControlCharacters`](#strings-and-composition) writes it, its `\uXXXX` escape, whose backslash is then written `\e`, so it shows rather than vanishes. Every other character above U+007F, a bidirectional control or mark included, as help prints it, is written `\[uXXXX]`, its code point in four or more uppercase hexadecimal digits, so a page is ASCII and reads the same whether or not the `man` program runs `preconv`.
- **Fonts.** A run of text in a font writes `\fB`, `\fI`, or `\f(BI` before it and `\fR` after it, so every line ends in the regular font, and a request line such as `.SS` or `.TP` holds no font escape.

#### Markdown in roff

`details` is parsed with the parser help uses, under the block and inline rules of [Markdown details](#markdown-details), and rendered in roff's own way: `man` fills a paragraph and wraps it to the reader's width, so the author's line breaks inside a paragraph are not kept, while code keeps every line. Spacing between blocks is the macro package's.

- **A paragraph** is its lines, each written as a source line, which `man` joins, after a `.PP` under Paragraph breaks.
- **A heading** at the top level of `details` is `.SS` and its text, its inline constructs printed as plain text. A heading inside a list item or a quote is a paragraph in bold.
- **Code** is `.RS 4`, `.nf`, its lines, `.fi`, and `.RE`, after a `.PP` under Paragraph breaks, dropping the blank lines at its start and end. Each line loses the whitespace at its end, as on help, and a line left empty is written `\&`, so the page holds no blank line and the code keeps its empty lines. Code with no other line prints nothing.
- **A thematic break** is a paragraph that holds it as written.
- **A list item** is `.IP` with its marker and the marker's width and one: `.IP \(bu 2` for every bullet, and for an ordered item its number, counting up by one from the first item's number with leading zeros dropped, and the author's delimiter, so `007.` gives `.IP 7. 3`. When the item's first block is a paragraph, or a heading, which prints as a paragraph in bold, its lines follow the `.IP`, and the item's other blocks follow in `.PP`, `.RS <width>`, and `.RE`; otherwise every block of the item is in `.RS <width>` and `.RE` right after the `.IP`. A nested list is therefore indented by its parent's marker.
- **A quote** is its blocks in `.RS 4` and `.RE`, after a `.PP` under Paragraph breaks.
- **Inline.** Emphasis is italic, strong emphasis is bold, and a code span is bold without its backticks, the man convention for a literal; the fonts combine, so a code span inside emphasis is bold italic. A link prints its text, a space, and its destination in angle brackets, `the format <https://www.json.org/json-en.html>`, or, when the text prints exactly as the destination, the text alone in its own fonts, and when it prints nothing but whitespace, the destination alone, so no text line starts with a space. An image prints as a link with the same text, and an autolink prints its address. A backslash escape prints its character, and everything else prints as written, as on help.

#### Writing the pages

- **`generate`.** `--out` is resolved against `host.cwd`. The plugin creates the folder and each missing parent with mode `755`, whatever the umask, then writes each page to a staging file it creates exclusively in the folder, named `.<file>.<random>.loom-staging`, with mode `644`, whatever the umask, and renames it into place, which replaces a file or a symbolic link of that name. It touches nothing else in the folder and records nothing, so `generate` runs on every platform, `win32` included, and from every build. It prints `Wrote <count> man pages to <folder>.` through `out.success`. A `--out` that names anything but a folder fails with a `FatalError` and exit 1 before anything is written: `/home/me/src/jsonkit/build/man is not a folder. Name a folder, or a path where jsonkit can create one.` A file system call that fails throws the runtime's error, which fails the run through the ordinary failure path, and the staging file is removed.
- **The folder.** `install` writes the set to `<home>/.local/share/man/man1`, where `<home>` is `HOME` from `host.env`. Neither man-db nor macOS's `man` reads `XDG_DATA_HOME`, and both search `<dir>/share/man` for each `<dir>/bin` on `PATH`, so a page there is found whenever `<home>/.local/bin`, the [installer script](toolchain.md#the-installer-script)'s default folder, is on `PATH`.
- **The record.** The set is recorded through the [installed-files module](#installed-files) in the plugin's file `manpage.json`, every page a file with its digest, under the module's rules as written: there is no `--force`, and each folder the module creates is created with mode `755` and each page written with mode `644`, whatever the umask.
- **Checks first.** Each of `install`, `update`, and `uninstall` checks, in this order, and fails at the first that fails:
  1. The platform. No platform refuses: on `win32` each child resolves its folder from `HOME` as on other platforms, under [ADR-0100](decisions/0100-acceptance-plans-live-beside-the-tests.md).
  2. `install`: `<home>`, which fails as [Skills](#global-installs) states when `HOME` is not an absolute path.
  3. The record's directory, `applicationDirectory('installation', name, host)`, which answering `{ variable }` fails as Skills states.
  4. The plugin's file, read through the module. One that is damaged or holds an unknown `format` fails with a `FatalError` and exit 1: `<record> cannot be read, so jsonkit will not change the man pages it lists. Remove it and the pages it lists, then run jsonkit manpage install again.`, with `uninstall` in place of `install` for that child.
  5. `install` and `update`: every page of the set, under Files the record does not list.
- **Files the record does not list.** A file, folder, or symbolic link at a page's path that `manpage.json` does not record, such as a page an earlier `generate` wrote there or a link a dotfile manager keeps, and a recorded page of the set, one this run would write, whose digest changed since it was written, each refuse `install` and `update`, which write nothing. A recorded page the set no longer holds never refuses; it is kept as `install` states. The child prints one line for each through `out.warn`, `<file> was not installed by jsonkit manpage install.` or `<file> changed since jsonkit manpage install wrote it.`, where `<file>` is the page's path, then fails with a `FatalError` and exit 1: `jsonkit manpage install changed nothing, because files it did not install are in the way.`, corrected by `Remove them, then run jsonkit manpage install again.` `update` uses `jsonkit manpage update` in the failure sentence and `jsonkit manpage install` in the correction.
- **`install`.** The module installs every page of the set. The set is unchanged when `manpage.json` is committed, records exactly the set's paths, and every page is a regular file at its path whose digest is the recorded one and the one it would hold; then nothing is written, and it prints `The <count> man pages in <folder> are unchanged.` through `out.info`. Otherwise it prints `Installed <count> man pages in <folder>.` through `out.success`, counting the whole set. A recorded page the set no longer holds, as when a Command was removed or hidden, or every recorded page after `HOME` changed while the record's directory stayed, as it does on Linux under an absolute `XDG_STATE_HOME`, so that the set moves to the new folder, is removed when its digest is unchanged and prints `Removed <file>.`, and is kept when it changed and prints `<file> changed since jsonkit manpage install wrote it, so it was left in place.` through `out.warn`. Then it prints `Read them with man jsonkit.` through `out.info`, or the advice below.
- **Advice when `man` will not find them.** After `install`, the plugin reads `MANPATH` and `PATH` from `host.env`. An entry of `PATH` maps to the folder when, with a trailing `/` removed, it is `<home>/.local/bin`. `man` finds `<home>/.local/share/man` when one of these holds:
  - `MANPATH` is unset or empty, and an entry of `PATH` maps to the folder;
  - `MANPATH` lists `<home>/.local/share/man`;
  - `MANPATH` holds an empty entry, at its start, at its end, or between two colons, which both `man` programs read as their default search, and an entry of `PATH` maps to the folder.

  When none holds, the plugin prints `man will not find these pages until MANPATH lists <home>/.local/share/man. Add this line to your shell's startup file:` through `out.warn`, then `export MANPATH="<home>/.local/share/man:${MANPATH-}"` through `out.print`, with each `"`, `\`, `$`, and `` ` `` in the folder escaped with a `\`. When the last segment of `SHELL` is `fish`, the line is `set -gx MANPATH '<home>/.local/share/man' "$MANPATH"` instead, with the folder in Fish's single quotes as [Completion](#completion) writes them: Fish joins a quoted path variable with colons, and reads an unset one as one empty element, which gives the trailing colon. When `MANPATH` was unset, the line leaves a trailing colon, so the default search still follows, and `${MANPATH-}` reads an unset variable as empty under `set -u`. The plugin never edits a startup file.
- **A new home on macOS.** On `darwin` the record's directory is under `HOME`, so after `HOME` changes the plugin reads the new home's record, and the pages under the old home stay where they are, recorded in the old home's record.
- **`update`.** It acts only on what `manpage.json` records, read as recovery would resolve it. It installs the set into the folder that holds the recorded pages and derives no page path from `HOME`, so a refresh run from another environment never moves a page. A record whose pages sit in more than one folder, which only an install interrupted while it moved the set leaves, fails `update` with a `FatalError` and exit 1 before anything is written: `<record> lists man pages in more than one folder, so jsonkit manpage update cannot tell where they belong. Run jsonkit manpage install to put them in one folder.` Otherwise it prints `Updated <count> man pages in <folder>.` in place of the installed line, or the unchanged line, with removed and kept pages as `install` prints them. It prints no advice. With no page recorded, it prints `jsonkit has no man pages installed, so there is nothing to update. Run jsonkit manpage install to install them.` through `out.success` and exits 0.
- **`uninstall`.** The module removes each recorded page whose digest is unchanged, keeps each changed one, removes each directory it created that is then empty, and deletes the plugin's file. It prints `Removed <count> man pages from <folder>.` through `out.success` for each folder it removed pages from, in the order the record lists them, counting that folder's pages, and each kept page prints the left-in-place line through `out.warn`. A recorded page already gone is not counted and prints nothing. When it removed and kept no page, as with no page recorded or every recorded page already gone, it prints `jsonkit has no man pages installed, so there is nothing to remove.` through `out.success` and exits 0.
- **Any build.** Every child acts from a `source`, `development`, or `distributed` build alike, because a page describes the graph, not the binary's path.
- **No index.** The plugin never runs `mandb` or `makewhatis`. `man <page>` finds an installed page without an index; `apropos` and `whatis` find it after the system's next index run.

#### Refreshing man pages after a self-update

`refreshManpages` is an `afterReplace` function for the [self-update plugin](#self-update), which passes it a context that holds every member `RefreshContext` names. A page is fixed text, so after a replace the installed pages describe the old version until they are rewritten, and the replaced process holds the old version's graph. `refreshManpages` therefore runs the new binary, and `update` decides what to refresh. It runs `path` with the words `manpage update` exactly as [`refreshSkills`](#refreshing-after-a-self-update) runs `skills update`, under the same rules for the child, its output, and the run signal. A child that fails, or that cannot start, adds the `warn` log event `Man pages were not refreshed after the update.`, with the same fields, and resolves; one that cannot start writes `The man pages were not refreshed because /home/me/.local/bin/jsonkit could not start. Run jsonkit manpage update.` to `host.stderr`. An application that also refreshes skills or completion calls each from its own `afterReplace`, as [Completion](#refreshing-completion-after-a-self-update) shows. A binary that a package manager, npm, or the installer script replaced runs no `afterReplace`, and its installed pages stay those of the earlier version until the operator runs `manpage update`.

- **Output.** A count of 1 reads `1 man page`, and every other count `man pages`. The `Wrote`, `Installed`, `Updated`, `Removed <count>`, and nothing-to lines go through `out.success`; the unchanged, `Removed <file>`, and `Read them` lines through `out.info`; the refused-file, left-in-place, and advice lines through `out.warn`; and the `export` line through `out.print`, the only thing a child writes to stdout. The examples above omit the glyph each lane view adds. Every path a sentence repeats passes through `escapeControlCharacters`. Every refusal and check failure above is a `FatalError` that exits 1, and a missing `--out` is core's usage error, with exit 2.
- **Names.** `manpage`, `refreshManpages`, and `RefreshContext` are exported from `@loomcli/plugins/manpage`. `RefreshContext` is the same declaration `@loomcli/plugins/skills` exports.

#### Man pages acceptance

Man pages are proven when public APIs alone produce these results under Node and Bun:

- **The page.** jsonkit installs `manpage()`, and `jsonkit manpage generate --out <folder>` writes `jsonkit-get.1` byte for byte as above, with jsonkit's version. Two runs, and a run under another `HOME`, `TERM`, `COLUMNS`, and locale, write identical bytes, and `generate` and `install` write identical pages. `groff -man -Tutf8 -ww -z` reads every page jsonkit writes with no warning, and where `mandoc` is on `PATH`, `mandoc -T lint -W warning` reports `missing date` for each page, which the empty date gives, and nothing else.
- **The set.** jsonkit's set holds a page for the root, each visible child, the deprecated `fetch`, and each visible plugin Command, and none for `debug`, `paths`, `__complete`, or the alias `ls`. The root page lists `fetch` with its deprecated fact and neither `debug` nor `paths`, and `jsonkit-fetch.1` opens its DESCRIPTION with `Deprecated: Use get instead.`
- **Sections.** A fixture covers each section and its omission: a root page whose GLOBAL OPTIONS hold jsonkit's globals and a child page that holds none and names `jsonkit(1)` under SEE ALSO; authored outer and inner help sections as `.SH` and `.SS` in help's order; a hidden option on neither OPTIONS nor ENVIRONMENT; an option with an environment binding and `configInput`, which prints both lines and an ENVIRONMENT entry; a Boolean of each polarity, a long-only option, a `shortOnly` option, a counted option, a string option with an implied value, and an option with a closed set, each tag with the pinned fonts and each text as help prints its row, and each ENVIRONMENT entry naming the pinned spelling; an example with a note and one without; a Command with no description, whose NAME is the page name alone and whose parent's entry for it writes its tag alone; and a root whose authored option section holds a global. An application that installs neither help nor the configuration plugin still writes every page, reading the values its Commands carry.
- **Markdown.** A unit test renders each block and inline construct of [Markdown details](#markdown-details) to the pinned roff: a paragraph's lines filled, a heading at the top level and inside a list item, fenced and indented code with blank lines at its ends, an empty line inside it, and a line ending in spaces, a thematic break, nested bullet and ordered lists with `007.` numbering and an item whose first block is code, a quote holding a list, a quote after a paragraph, an item with two paragraphs, emphasis, strong emphasis, a code span inside emphasis, a link, a link whose text is its destination, an image, and an autolink.
- **Escapes.** A description, a details paragraph and heading, an authored help section heading, a code line, an example, and a version each holding a leading `.`, a `'`, a `"`, a `` ` ``, a `^`, a `~`, a `\`, `\fB`, a `-`, an escape character, and non-ASCII text such as `café — 中` render under `groff -man -Tutf8` as the characters written, the quote kept in a heading and the ASCII characters as ASCII, with the escape character shown as `\u001b`; a tab inside a code line renders as space up to a tab stop, and one in a description as a space. Every page is ASCII, and `groff -man -Tutf8 -ww -z` reports nothing.
- **Names that collide.** Fixtures with a root child `foo-bar` beside `foo bar`, and with `Get` beside `get`, fail every build with the pinned diagnostic under `@loomcli/plugins/manpage/page-name-taken`, and the same graph with one of the two hidden builds.
- **Generating.** `generate` creates a missing folder and its parents with mode `755` and pages with mode `644` under umask `077`, replaces a page of the same name and a symbolic link of that name, leaves every other file, writes no installation record, and runs on a `win32` fixture host. A `--out` that names a file fails with the pinned sentence and writes nothing, and a run without `--out` exits 2.
- **Installing.** Process tests set `HOME`, `XDG_STATE_HOME`, and the working directory to temporary directories, and clear `MANPATH` and `SHELL` unless a case sets them:
  - `install` writes the set under `<home>/.local/share/man/man1` with the modes above, records it in `manpage.json`, and prints the pinned lines; a second `install` prints the unchanged line and changes no byte. Where `man` is on `PATH`, `man -w jsonkit-get` with `MANPATH` unset and `<home>/.local/bin` on `PATH` prints the installed page's path.
  - With `PATH` lacking `<home>/.local/bin`, and with `MANPATH` set to a list without the folder or an empty entry, `install` prints the pinned advice and the `export` line on stdout, and that line, run by `bash -u` with `MANPATH` unset and set, leaves the folder first on `MANPATH`; with `SHELL` ending in `fish`, it prints the Fish line, which a real Fish, where one is on `PATH`, runs to the same `MANPATH`; with `MANPATH` ending in a colon and `<home>/.local/bin` on `PATH`, it prints `Read them with man jsonkit.`
  - A page `generate` wrote into the folder, a symbolic link at a page's path, and a recorded page edited since, each refuse `install` and `update` with exit 1, print the refused line, and change no byte. After an installed page is deleted, `install` writes it again and prints the installed line. After an `install` killed once every page was written and before the record was committed, the next `install` recovers the record and prints the installed line.
  - On a `linux` host, after `HOME` changes with `XDG_STATE_HOME` held, `install` writes the set under the new home and removes the unchanged pages under the old one, printing a removed line for each. A record left with pages in both folders by an `install` killed while moving fails `update` with the pinned sentence, `uninstall` removes both folders' pages with one removed line for each folder, and the next `install` puts the set in one folder.
  - After a Command is removed from the fixture, `install` and `update` remove its unchanged page and keep an edited one with the left-in-place line. After a Command is added, `update` writes its page into the recorded folder, and on a `linux` host it does so even with `HOME` changed since and `XDG_STATE_HOME` held.
  - With nothing recorded, `update` and `uninstall` print their nothing-to lines and exit 0, and with every recorded page already deleted, `uninstall` prints its nothing-to-remove line, deletes `manpage.json`, and exits 0. `uninstall` removes every unchanged page and each created directory then empty, deletes `manpage.json`, keeps an edited page with the pinned warning, and leaves a `man1` folder that held another file.
  - A damaged `manpage.json` fails each child with the pinned sentence and writes nothing, and a `win32` fixture host fails `install` with the pinned sentence, while `update` and `uninstall` print their nothing-to lines and exit 0.
- **Refreshing.** `refreshManpages`, given a fixture binary path, runs it with `manpage update`, pipes its output into the host's streams, and resolves; a child that exits 1, and a path that cannot start, each add the pinned `warn` log event and resolve. Installed as `selfUpdate({ afterReplace: refreshManpages })` under the self-update fixture, an update rewrites a recorded page to the replaced binary's version.
- **Packed consumers.** A consumer installs the packed pack, imports `@loomcli/plugins/manpage`, compiles against its declaration, and generates the pages.

### MCP

```ts
// @loomcli/plugins/mcp
import type { Plugin } from '@loomcli/core';

export declare function mcp(): Plugin;
```

```ts
// @loomcli/plugins/mcp/extension, declarations alone
import type { Extension, StandardSchemaV1 } from '@loomcli/core';

// The value an author gives mcpCommand.
// The package exports no name for this shape.
interface McpCommandInput {
  readonly description?: string; // the tool's description, in place of the Command's
  readonly annotations?: {
    readonly readOnly?: boolean; // projected as readOnlyHint
    readonly destructive?: boolean; // projected as destructiveHint
    readonly idempotent?: boolean; // projected as idempotentHint
    readonly openWorld?: boolean; // projected as openWorldHint
  };
}
export declare const mcpCommand: Extension<'command', StandardSchemaV1<McpCommandInput>>;
export declare const mcpInput: Extension<'option', StandardSchemaV1<{ readonly description: string }>>;
export declare const mcpArgument: Extension<'argument', StandardSchemaV1<{ readonly description: string }>>;
```

```ts
import { Application, Command } from '@loomcli/core';
import { mcp } from '@loomcli/plugins/mcp';
import { mcpArgument, mcpCommand } from '@loomcli/plugins/mcp/extension';

import { getValue } from './actions/get-value.js';

export const get = new Command('get', {
  description: 'Read one value at a path.',
  extensions: [mcpCommand({ annotations: { openWorld: false, readOnly: true } })],
})
  .argument('path', {
    description: 'Dot path to read.',
    extensions: [mcpArgument({ description: 'A dot-separated path from the document root, such as user.name.' })],
    required: true,
  })
  .option('file', {
    description: 'The document to read.',
    required: true,
    short: 'f',
    stdin: true,
    type: 'content',
  })
  .action(getValue);

export const jsonkit = new Application('jsonkit', { plugins: [mcp()] }).command(get);
```

An MCP client launches `jsonkit mcp` and speaks one JSON-RPC message per line over its stdin and stdout. Against jsonkit itself, whose `get` declares a local native content `--file` and whose Application declares its version and description, the first line below is the client's request and the second is the server's answer:

```text
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"method":"tools/call","params":{"_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion":"2026-07-28","io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities":{}},"name":"get","arguments":{"path":"user.name","file":"doc.json"}}}
{"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":1,"result":{"resultType":"complete","content":[{"type":"text","text":"\"Ada\"\n"}],"isError":false,"_meta":{"io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo":{"name":"jsonkit","version":"0.9.0","description":"Read and reshape one JSON document."}}}}
```

`mcp()` is the MCP plugin. It serves every Command that opts in as one tool of a [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28) server over stdio, and it runs each tool call through [`invoke`](#invocation-by-name), so a call is the Command's own run with the same validation, failures, and exit codes. MCP is a projection: a tool listing is the graph's facts for the Commands that opted in, and nothing in core knows the protocol. The protocol itself lives in a private package the plugin pack compiles into its own files. [ADR-0063](decisions/0063-the-mcp-plugin-serves-opted-in-commands-as-tools.md) records the decision.

- **The plugin.** Its identity is `@loomcli/plugins/mcp`. `mcp()` takes no settings and declares no option, no middleware, and no view, and it claims no slot. It contributes one [plugin Command](#plugin-commands), the three extensions above, and an [`onGraphBuilt`](#judging-the-built-graph) hook. The Command is `mcp`, visible, with the description `Serve this application's tools to an MCP client over stdin and stdout.`, no arguments, no options, and no result. A root that declares arguments cannot hold children, so such an application cannot install the plugin, the limit [completion](#completion) has under [ADR-0033](decisions/0033-a-plugin-attaches-ordinary-commands-to-the-root.md).
- **Opt-in.** A Command is a tool when it carries an `mcpCommand` value, and only then. The root opts in through the Application's `extensions`. An explicit opt-in wins over `hidden`, so a hidden Command that carries the value is a tool, and the listing in help, the manifest, and completion still omits it. A deprecated Command that opts in is a tool whose description opens with its migration message. An alias is never a tool and never a second name. A Command with no action cannot serve a call, so `mcpCommand` on a group is a build fault.
- **Tool names.** A tool's name is the Command's path joined by `_`, with each `-` written as `_`, so `scratch create` is `scratch_create` and `cache clear-all` is `cache_clear_all`. The root's tool is the application name written the same way, so `git-lfs` serves `git_lfs`. A [portable name](glossary.md#names-and-routing) holds nothing else the protocol's tool-name characters exclude, and `.` stays. There is no name override. Two opted-in Commands that give one name, such as the root and a child named like the application, are a build fault that names both.
- **The description.** A tool's description is the `mcpCommand` value's `description`, or else the Command's core `description`, the Application's at the root. With neither, the tool carries no description. A deprecated Command's description opens with `Deprecated: ` and its migration message, then a line break and the rest. The `mcpCommand` value's `description` is prose under the pack's prose rule: every line holds a character other than whitespace, and line breaks are kept. A core description and a migration message are one line each, so each line break the author wrote in one, CRLF or a single terminator, reads as one space; an input's core description and the server identity's description read the same way.
- **Annotations.** `annotations` projects onto the protocol's tool annotations, `readOnly` as `readOnlyHint`, `destructive` as `destructiveHint`, `idempotent` as `idempotentHint`, and `openWorld` as `openWorldHint`. An unset hint is omitted, so the protocol's own defaults apply, and a tool with none set carries no `annotations`. They are hints the author owns and Loom never verifies: Loom infers none from the graph, and nothing but this plugin reads them, neither core nor help nor the manifest. A false claim is a defect in the author's application, and the protocol tells a client to treat annotations from a server it does not trust as untrusted.
- **The input schema.** A tool's `inputSchema` is `{ type: 'object', properties, required, additionalProperties: false }`, with `required` left out when it is empty. `properties` holds every argument of the routed Command in declaration order, then its local options in authoring order, then every global option in graph order, keyed by declared name, minus a [hidden](#hidden-and-deprecated-members) option and a [control option](#control-options). Passthrough is never exposed.
  - Each property is the input's [input schema](#input-schema) without its top-level `$schema` key, because the property lives inside a schema whose dialect is the protocol's default, JSON Schema 2020-12, the target the converter answers. Where the graph holds `null`, the property is derived from the node: `{ type: 'string' }` for a string option or an argument, `{ type: 'boolean' }` for a Boolean option, and `{ type: 'integer', minimum: 0 }` for a counted option. A multiple option or a variadic argument wraps its value's schema as `{ type: 'array', items: <schema> }`.
  - The plugin sets `description` from the input's `mcpInput` or `mcpArgument` value, or else its core description, and a deprecated option's opens with `Deprecated: ` and its message, as a tool's does. It sets `default` from a declared default that is plain JSON data and leaves it out otherwise. Either key replaces one the converter wrote.
  - `required` lists each required argument and each required local option, in property order, a local option that declares `required: 'non-interactive'` included, because a tool call is never [interactive](#interaction). A global option is never required.
  - A Command whose tool would list an argument and an option under one name, a global option included, is a build fault, because a tool's arguments are one object. An author's argument and option may share a name everywhere else.
- **A call.** `tools/call` names a tool and passes `arguments`, an object or nothing. The plugin checks each key against the tool's `properties`: a key outside them, a hidden or control option's name included, is a tool execution error whose text is `Tool "get" takes no argument "x". Use a property its input schema lists.`, as the one text item with `isError: true` and no `structuredContent`, and no run starts. Otherwise the plugin splits the object, a key that names an argument going under `args` and every other key under `options`, and calls `invoke(path, { args, options }, { failure, signal, view })`. `view` is the first view, in record order, whose [media type](#media-types) is `application/json`, and it is omitted when the Command declares no result or no such view. `signal` is the call's own, which `notifications/cancelled` aborts. Values are not checked against the schema: [lowering](#invocation-by-name), the validators, and the run's own faults judge them and report by name.
- **A completed call.** `isError` is `false`, and `content` holds `output` as one text item and then `messages` as another, each only when it is not empty, or one empty text item when both are. When the view the plugin selected declares `application/json`, `structuredContent` is `output` parsed as JSON, any JSON value; when `output` does not parse, because a view's media type is a promise core never checks, the result carries the text alone. A `jsonl` view's output stays text. No content item carries annotations.
- **A failed call.** `isError` is `true`, and `content` holds `messages`, then any partial `output`, each only when it is not empty. The text is the failure's own report, by build, with no command-line hint, so a model reads what went wrong and what to do instead, and a defect in a distributed build reads the generic defect message. `structuredContent` is what the plugin's failure handler returns, `{ exitCode, failure }`: the outcome's exit code and the handler context's [failure form](#the-failure-form), `{ code, exitCode, message, hints }`. The form follows the build, so a defect in a distributed build reads `internal` and `Something went wrong.`, and its hints are the by-name hints, with no command-line hint. The handler exposes no cause and no stack. With both `messages` and `output` empty, as under an override view that renders nothing, `content` holds one empty text item, as a completed call's does.
- **Progress.** When a `tools/call` request carries `params._meta.progressToken`, a string or a number, the plugin passes `onProgress` to that call's `invoke`, and each [progress event](#progress-events) of the call becomes one `notifications/progress` on the token. `progress` is always a per-call counter, the number of events the call has delivered, this one included, so every event is sent and `progress` always increases. The notification carries no `total`. `message` carries the event's label, its counts, and its state, joined by single spaces: the label when it is not empty, then the counts when the event carries `completed`, `completed/total` with a total and `completed` alone without one, and no counts for an event that carries `total` without `completed`, each number written as JavaScript's `String` writes it, then the state in parentheses, such as `Fetching packages 3/8 (updated)`, `Fetching packages 8/8 (ended)`, `Building the index (started)`, or `(started)` for an event with no label and no counts. Progress lines that run at once in one call share its token and its counter. A call without a token passes no observer and receives no notification. The [protocol package](#the-protocol-package) sends none after the call's response or its cancellation, so a cancelled call's `cancelled` event sends nothing. The progress line's start and end lines still land in `messages`, which the result carries as text. The protocol stays pinned to `2026-07-28`, and discovery declares no new capability.
- **A cancelled call.** The server sends no response for it, as the protocol asks.
- **Protocol errors.** The plugin answers these as JSON-RPC errors rather than tool results, because no run started:

  | Request                                                | Error                                                                                       |
  | ------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
  | `tools/call` naming no tool the server lists           | `-32602`, `Unknown tool "gte". Call tools/list for the tool names.`                         |
  | `tools/call` whose `arguments` is not an object        | `-32602`, `Tool "get" arguments must be an object. Supply a JSON object of named inputs.` |
  | `tools/list` with a `cursor`                           | `-32602`, `The cursor is not one this server issued. Call tools/list without a cursor.`     |
  | Every protocol rule of the private package             | The codes [The protocol package](#the-protocol-package) states                              |

- **Discovery.** `server/discover` answers `supportedVersions: ['2026-07-28']`, `capabilities: { tools: {} }`, with no `listChanged` because the tool list never changes while the process runs, and no `logging`, `prompts`, `resources`, or `completions` capability. The application's identity is the server's: every result's `_meta` carries `io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo` as `{ name, version, description }`, the graph's `name` and `version` and the Application's description, which is left out when it declares none. The result carries no `instructions`, because Loom holds no fact that guides a model beyond the descriptions.
- **The listing.** `tools/list` answers every tool in one page, in graph order: the root first, then each Command depth first in authoring order. It carries no `nextCursor`. `server/discover` and `tools/list` each carry `ttlMs: 0` and `cacheScope: 'private'`, so a client caches neither: a client may outlive the server process, and the next process may serve a newer application whose tools differ.
- **Concurrency.** Calls may overlap. Each runs through its own `invoke`, and the server writes each response when its call settles. Loom adds no queue, limit, or timer, so an application whose actions cannot overlap serializes its own work.
- **The server's life.** The `mcp` action reads `host.stdin` and writes `host.stdout`, and stdout carries protocol messages alone, each written whole. The server writes no log of its own, and stderr carries dotenv warnings when that plugin is installed, a fault the `mcp` run itself reports and what an installed [`onLog`](#observing-log-events) hook writes to its destination's stderr, such as the [logging plugin](#logging-plugin)'s console records. When stdin ends, the server aborts every call in flight and answers none of them, waits for each to settle, ends each open subscription with its closing response, and returns, so the run exits 0. When the run's signal aborts, through a caller or a [signals owner](#signals-and-cancellation), every call's signal aborts with it, the server answers nothing more, and the run resolves its cancellation code. A plugin that writes to stdout on a run it does not own breaks the stream, as it breaks [completion](#completion)'s answer.
- **Names.** `mcp` is exported from `@loomcli/plugins/mcp`, and `mcpCommand`, `mcpInput`, and `mcpArgument` from `@loomcli/plugins/mcp/extension`, whose identities are `@loomcli/plugins/mcp/command`, `@loomcli/plugins/mcp/input`, and `@loomcli/plugins/mcp/argument`. `mcpCommand` is an ordinary extension, so a later value replaces an earlier one. The pack's public declarations name no protocol type.

#### MCP build faults

The plugin's `onGraphBuilt` hook judges the opted-in Commands on every build, a run that never serves a tool included, and throws a `DeclarationError` under a rule of its own, which reports as itself under [Judging the built graph](#judging-the-built-graph). A sentence names the root as `the root Command`, capitalized where it opens the sentence, in place of a quoted path.

| Rejected declaration | Diagnostic | Rule |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Two opted-in Commands that give one tool name | `Commands "scratch create" and "scratch_create" both serve the MCP tool "scratch_create". Rename one Command, or remove mcpCommand from one of them.` | `@loomcli/plugins/mcp/tool-name-taken` |
| `mcpCommand` on a Command with no action | `Command "cache" carries mcpCommand and registers no action. Remove mcpCommand, or opt in the Commands under it.` | `@loomcli/plugins/mcp/tool-without-action` |
| An argument and an option a tool would list under one name | `Command "get" declares argument "path" and option "path", which one MCP tool lists under one name. Rename one of them, or remove mcpCommand.` A global option reads `global option "path"`. | `@loomcli/plugins/mcp/property-name-taken` |

#### The protocol package

The protocol is written in this repository, in the private workspace package `@loom/mcp` at `packages/mcp`, which is never published. It knows MCP and nothing of Loom, and the plugin speaks MCP only through it.

- **One revision.** The package holds one named constant, the protocol revision `2026-07-28`, and the protocol types of that revision alone. Moving to a later revision is a deliberate change to this package and the plugin's tests, never a dependency update.
- **Framing.** The stdio transport reads newline-delimited JSON-RPC 2.0 messages and writes each message as one line of `JSON.stringify` output with no indentation, followed by a line feed, so no message holds an embedded line break. A blank line, one that holds nothing but spaces, tabs, and carriage returns, is ignored. Any other line that is not JSON is answered with `-32700`, and a message that is not a JSON-RPC request or notification, a batch included, with `-32600`. A response from the client is ignored. A last line that ends without a line feed when stdin ends is read as one message.
- **Request ids.** A request whose id matches a call or a subscription still in flight is answered, before every other check, with `-32600` and a message naming the id in use, such as `The request id 7 is in use by a request still in flight. Send each request with an id no request in flight holds.` The request in flight keeps the id and runs untouched, so its answer stays the only one under that id and shutdown still waits for it. An id is free again once its request settles or the client cancels it.
- **Per-request checks.** Every request carries `io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion` and `io.modelcontextprotocol/clientCapabilities` in its `params._meta`, and the server relies on no earlier request. A request missing either is answered with `-32602`. A request for any version other than `2026-07-28` is answered with `UnsupportedProtocolVersionError`, `-32022`, whose `data` is `{ supported: ['2026-07-28'], requested }`.
- **A legacy client.** An `initialize` request is answered, before the checks above, with `-32022` and `data` `{ supported: ['2026-07-28'], requested }`, where `requested` is the request's own `protocolVersion` when it holds a string and `""` otherwise, because the protocol requires the field, and with the message `Unsupported protocol version. This server speaks MCP 2026-07-28, which has no initialize request; use a client that supports protocol version 2026-07-28.` A client that speaks both eras probes with `server/discover` and never sends it.
- **Methods.** The package serves `server/discover`, `tools/list`, `tools/call`, and `subscriptions/listen`, answers every other method, `ping` included, with `-32601` before the per-request checks, so a `ping` without `_meta` answers `-32601`, and stamps `resultType: 'complete'` and the server's identity in `_meta` on every result. `subscriptions/listen` is acknowledged by `notifications/subscriptions/acknowledged`, its first message, with an empty `notifications` filter and `_meta['io.modelcontextprotocol/subscriptionId']` set to the request's id, and the server sends no other notification on it, because it offers no notification type. It stays open until the client cancels it or the server shuts down. A `tools/call` whose `params.name` is not a string is answered with `-32602`. A throw while the server handles a request is answered with `-32603`, and the server keeps serving.
- **Cancellation.** `notifications/cancelled` aborts the request it names and suppresses its response. A notification for an unknown or settled request is ignored. Every other notification is ignored.
- **Progress.** A `tools/call` handler receives a function that sends progress when the request's `params._meta` carries a `progressToken`, a string or a number, and no function otherwise. Each call of it writes one `notifications/progress` whose params hold the token as `progressToken`, the given `progress`, and the given `total` and `message` when present, and the package passes each one on as given, because its caller keeps `progress` increasing as the protocol requires. It writes none once the call is answered, cancelled by the client, or aborted by shutdown or the run's signal.
- **Shutdown.** When stdin ends, the package stops reading, aborts every call in flight, waits for each to settle, sends `notifications/cancelled` naming each open subscription, answers it with its closing result, whose `_meta` carries `io.modelcontextprotocol/subscriptionId` beside the server's identity, and resolves, so the caller returns. A call shutdown aborts answers nothing, as a call the client cancels answers nothing, while a `server/discover` or `tools/list` still pending is answered. A write the client can no longer read, such as one after it closed its end of the pipe, is dropped, and the run still resolves.
- **The run's signal.** `run(input, output, { signal })` takes an optional `AbortSignal`, through which the caller ends the run early. When it aborts, before or after stdin ends, the package stops reading, aborts every call, answers nothing more, an open subscription's closing result included, and resolves once each call has settled. A signal already aborted when the run starts ends it before it reads anything.
- **Bundled into the pack.** `@loomcli/plugins` lists `@loom/mcp` as a development dependency alone. The pack keeps `tsc` for every subpath, and its build then bundles the `mcp` subpath's emitted entry with Rolldown, inlining `@loom/mcp` and leaving `@loomcli/core` and the pack's own modules external, so the packed tarball names no dependency on the private package.

#### MCP acceptance

The protocol package is proven when its own conformance tests, which import nothing of Loom, produce these results under Node and Bun:

- **The constant.** The package exports one revision, `2026-07-28`, and every version check and answer reads it.
- **Framing.** A message split across two reads parses once, two messages in one read parse in order, a blank line is ignored, a line that is not JSON answers `-32700`, a batch and a JSON value that is not a request answer `-32600`, and every line the server writes parses as one message and holds no raw line break.
- **Discovery and versions.** `server/discover` answers the fields above with `ttlMs` and `cacheScope`. A request without `_meta`, or missing either required key, answers `-32602`, a request for `2025-11-25` answers `-32022` naming `2026-07-28` and the requested version, `initialize` answers `-32022` with the message above, and `ping` and an unknown method answer `-32601`.
- **Tools.** `tools/list` answers with `resultType`, `ttlMs`, `cacheScope`, and no `nextCursor`, a cursor answers `-32602`, and `tools/call` reaches the handler it was given with the request's name and arguments.
- **Request ids.** A request reusing the id of a call or a subscription in flight answers `-32600` naming the id, the first call runs on untouched, and the id serves again once its request settles or is cancelled.
- **Cancellation.** A cancelled request's handler sees its signal abort and no response is written, and a cancellation for an unknown or settled id changes nothing.
- **Subscriptions and shutdown.** `subscriptions/listen` is acknowledged first by `notifications/subscriptions/acknowledged` with an empty filter and the subscription's id in `_meta`, a client's cancellation ends it with no response, and closing stdin aborts calls in flight, answers none of them, waits for each to settle, sends `notifications/cancelled` naming the subscription, ends it with its closing result carrying its id in `_meta`, and resolves. A client that stops reading before stdin ends leaves the run to resolve and the process to exit 0.
- **The run's signal.** A signal already aborted resolves the run with nothing read or written, and a signal that aborts while a call and a subscription are open aborts the call, writes nothing more, and resolves with stdin still open, as it does after stdin has ended.
- **Progress.** A call whose `_meta` carries a progress token, a string and a number each, receives a progress function, and each call of it writes one `notifications/progress` with the token and the given values, in call order. A `total` or `message` left out is absent from the params, and nothing is written after the call's response, after its cancellation, or after shutdown. A call without a token receives no function.

The plugin is proven when jsonkit installs `mcp()` and opts in its root, `get`, `keys`, and `select`, each with `annotations: { openWorld: false, readOnly: true }`, and leaves `fetch`, `debug`, and `paths` out, and public APIs alone produce these results under Node and Bun:

- **A real session.** A process test launches the built `jsonkit mcp` under Node and under Bun and drives a session over stdio: `server/discover` names `jsonkit`, its version, and its description; `tools/list` lists `jsonkit`, `get`, `keys`, and `select` in that order with the schemas above, `file` among each tool's properties, and no `help`, `version`, `manifest`, `format`, `explain`, `color`, `verbose`, or `quiet` property; and a call of each tool against a document file answers as below. Closing stdin ends the process with exit 0.
- **Results.** `get` answers the value as text with no `structuredContent`; `jsonkit` answers the root's members as text and as `structuredContent`, the array its `json` view prints; `select` with an absent field answers the fields as text and the warning as a second text item; and a missing path answers `isError: true` with `Path not found: "missing". Run jsonkit keys to list the keys at the root.` and `structuredContent` `{ exitCode: 65, failure: { code: 'path-not-found', exitCode: 65, message: 'Path not found: "missing". Run jsonkit keys to list the keys at the root.', hints: [] } }`.
- **Errors.** An unknown tool and non-object arguments answer `-32602`. A key outside the schema answers the plugin's tool execution error. A value of the wrong shape and a missing required argument answer `isError: true` with the by-name sentence, no help hint, and a form whose code is `invalid-input`, and a malformed document answers 65 with the code `invalid-json`. A fixture tool whose action throws a `TypeError` answers the form `internal` with `Something went wrong.` from a bundle.
- **Cancellation and concurrency.** A fixture tool that waits on its signal is cancelled by `notifications/cancelled` and answers nothing while a second call answers. Two overlapping calls answer by their own ids. A run cancelled through a caller signal aborts both calls in flight.
- **Progress.** A fixture tool with a progress line of total 3 that updates to 1, 2, and 3 and ends, called with a progress token, sends five `notifications/progress` with `progress` 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5, none with a `total`, and the messages `Fetching records 0/3 (started)`, `Fetching records 1/3 (updated)`, `Fetching records 2/3 (updated)`, `Fetching records 3/3 (updated)`, and `Fetching records 3/3 (ended)`, before its result, whose text holds the start and end lines. A spinner line that starts, changes its label once, and ends sends `progress` 1, 2, and 3. A spinner line `Fetching records` that ends with the message `Fetched 3 records.` sends `Fetching records (started)` and `Fetched 3 records. (ended)`. Two lines that each start and end in one call share the token and one counter, so their four notifications read `progress` 1 to 4 in the order their events were delivered, and none is left out. The same call without a token sends no notification, and a call the client cancels sends none after its cancellation. A hand-drawn region that reports `{ completed: 1 }` with no label sends the message `1 (started)`, and one that reports `{}` sends `(started)`.
- **Fixtures.** Fixture applications prove a hidden Command that opts in listed, a deprecated one listed with its message opening the description, an alias never listed, a description and a property description override, annotations projected and omitted, the three build faults with their diagnostics in both builds, a property derived for each kind of input with a `null` schema, an array property for a multiple option, a mapped `json` view under another key chosen for `structuredContent`, a view under `application/json` whose text does not parse answering text alone, and the install refused on a root that declares arguments.
- **Packed consumers.** `check:packed` installs the packed pack, imports `@loomcli/plugins/mcp` and `@loomcli/plugins/mcp/extension`, compiles against their declarations, finds no `@loom/mcp` among the tarball's dependencies or in any of its built files, and serves an MCP session from a fixture application under Node and Bun.

### Suggestions

```ts
// @loomcli/plugins/suggestions
import type { Plugin } from '@loomcli/core';

export declare function suggestions(): Plugin;
```

```ts
import { Application } from '@loomcli/core';
import { help } from '@loomcli/plugins/help';
import { suggestions } from '@loomcli/plugins/suggestions';

export const jsonkit = new Application('jsonkit', { plugins: [help(), suggestions()] });
```

```text
$ jsonkit gte name -f doc.json
jsonkit: Unknown command "gte". Did you mean "get"?
Run "jsonkit --help" to see the usage.
```

`suggestions()` is the suggestions plugin. Its identity is `@loomcli/plugins/suggestions`, and it declares no options, no middleware, no extension, and no Command. Its contribution is one `onFailure` hook and two view overrides, for `UnknownCommandError` and for `UnknownOptionError`, listed under its `views` and resolved as [Views from plugins](#views-from-plugins) resolves any override. A failure view's context carries no graph, under [ADR-0046](decisions/0046-a-failure-view-reads-where-the-run-was-and-plugins-add-hint-lines.md), so the hook is where the plugin reads one: for either class it reads `graph` and `command` under [Failure hints](#failure-hints), computes the matches, records them for that failure instance in a module-private `WeakMap`, and returns `undefined`, so it adds no hint. Core hands the hook and the view one failure instance and runs the hook first, so the view reads the matches the hook recorded, and finds none for a failure no hook ran for. A suggestion is the near match the plugin's view offers as the failure's fix. Core's own sentence never guesses, under rule 3 of [Failure messages](failure-messages.md#3-leave-plugin-pointers-to-hint-lines): it lists the declared children and says what to do instead. A wrong guess is the plugin's risk, taken by the application that installs it. The matcher is a private module of the plugin, and the pack exports no matching function.

- **The sentence.** With at least one match, the view writes the prefix core's default text writes for a usage error, then the sentence's first clause with the token or spelling escaped through [`escapeControlCharacters`](#strings-and-composition) and then `style.escape`, under rule 5 of [Failure messages](failure-messages.md#5-escape-everything-repeated), `Unknown command "gte". ` or `Unknown option "--fields". `, then the fix: `Did you mean "get"?` for one match, and `Did you mean one of these: get, keys?` for several, in rank order, separated by a comma and a space. A name prints as declared: a child's canonical name, or an option's long or negative spelling with its dashes. Neither the `Use one of` clause nor the `prefix a hyphenated path with "./"` clause prints, because the suggestion is the fix. The line ends with one newline, and then each hint under [Failure hints](#failure-hints) follows on its own line, exactly as core's default text prints hints. Nothing in the line is styled.
- **No match.** With no candidate inside the budget, the view writes core's default text for the failure, hints included, byte for byte, so installing the plugin changes nothing for a token that resembles nothing. The view composes both shapes from the context's `application` and `style.escape(failure.message)`, the sentence without its prefix escaped as core's default text escapes its whole line, so it calls nothing of core's and matches core's text by construction, a token holding a control or bidirectional character included.
- **Candidates.** For an unknown Command, the canonical names of `command.children`, where `command` is the last Command the partial path reached, so `store cache lst`, on an application with a `cache` group, matches against the children of `cache`. For an unknown option, the long spelling and, for a Boolean, the negative spelling of each option in `graph.globals` and then `command.options`, so a counted option offers its long spelling alone, the routed Command's own, so a plugin's option is a candidate and `--hlep` suggests `--help`. A hidden member, a deprecated member, and every alias are left out, by the node facts, the rule [completion](#completion) follows under [ADR-0043](decisions/0043-shell-completion-follows-cobras-protocol-and-never-evaluates-typed-text.md): a typo of a deprecated Command suggests nothing unless a visible sibling is near, and an alias is never matched, so a typo of `ls` does not reach `keys` through it, and a typo of an option's alias does not reach that option through it. A short spelling is never a candidate, because one letter sits below any useful distance, so an unknown short spelling gets core's text. An option's long and negative spellings are both compared, and the option offers only the nearer of the two, or both in graph order when the typed spelling is as near to each, so `--no-colr` and `--nocolor` suggest `--no-color` and never `--color`, and `--noclor`, two edits from each, suggests both.
- **The matcher.** The typed token and each candidate are normalized to NFC and lowercased with the locale-independent default conversion before the comparison, so `GET` matches `get` at distance 0 and `Bild` reaches a `Build` Command, and a match prints as declared. Lengths and distances count code points, after folding. For an option, the leading hyphens of the typed spelling and of each candidate are left out of the comparison and of the length, so `--fields` is six code points against `field`. A token shorter than two code points after that matches nothing. The distance is the restricted Damerau-Levenshtein distance, also called optimal string alignment: an insertion, a deletion, a substitution, and a transposition of two adjacent code points each cost 1, so `gte` is one edit from `get`. The budget depends on the typed token's length: a token of up to 4 code points allows a distance of 1, up to 8 allows 2, and a longer token allows 3. A spelling inside the budget is a match, and an option offers only its nearer spelling, as the candidates rule above states. Matches rank by ascending distance, and ties keep graph order: the authoring order of `command.children` for a Command, and `graph.globals` then `command.options` for an option, with one option's long spelling ahead of its negative spelling. At most three names print. Every constant is the plugin's own, so a change to one is a text change under [Change fragments](../.changes/README.md), not a breaking one.
- **Precedence.** The application's overrides resolve first, then each plugin's in installation order, so an application that overrides `UnknownCommandError`, `UnknownOptionError`, or a class above them such as `UsageError` owns that sentence and prints no suggestion, and an earlier-installed plugin's override of either class or of a class above them wins over this plugin's. The plugin has no middleware, so its position in `plugins` changes no takeover and no chain order; the contract places no rule on where it is installed.
