- **Loading the files.** `install` and `update` call each skill's `files` once, in declaration order, after every check under Global installs or Project installs that comes before loading, and before they read the record or write anything, and await each; `uninstall` calls no loader, so a broken loader never blocks a removal. A loader that throws or rejects fails the run through the ordinary [failure path](#failure-contract). The result is judged before anything is written, and the first fault throws a `DeclarationError` of `@loomcli/plugins/skills/files`, which fails the run through the same path:

  | The result | The sentence and correction |
  | --- | --- |
  | not an array, or holding an entry whose `path` is not a string or whose `content` is neither a string nor a `Uint8Array` | `Skill "notes" loaded something that is not a list of files.`, corrected by `Return a list of { path, content } files from the skill's files function.` |
  | a path that is empty, starts with `/`, holds `\` or a control character, or has an empty, `.`, or `..` segment | `Skill "notes" lists a file path that is not a plain relative path: ../notes.md.`, corrected by `Use a relative path with / between its parts and no empty, ., or .. part, such as references/commands.md.` |
  | a path a second entry repeats | `Skill "notes" lists the file references/commands.md twice.`, corrected by `List each file once.` |
  | no entry whose path is `SKILL.md` | `Skill "notes" lists no SKILL.md.`, corrected by `Add the skill's SKILL.md at the top of its files.` |

  A path the sentence repeats passes through `escapeControlCharacters`. The plugin judges no file's content.
- **The Commands.** `skills`, visible, with the description `Install this application's agent skills.`, and three children, each visible with no arguments:
  - `install`, `Install the skills for your coding agents.`, with the string option `--agent`, `The agents to install for: claude, or agents for Codex and others. Both when left out.`, validated to `claude` or `agents`; the Boolean option `--project`, `Install into the current repository instead of your home folder.`; the string option `--directory` with the short spelling `-C`, `Find the repository from this directory instead of the current one.`; and the Boolean option `--force`, `Replace skill files that something else wrote or that you changed.`
  - `update`, `Bring installed skills up to date with this version.`, with no options.
  - `uninstall`, `Remove the skills from your coding agents.`, with `--agent`, `The agents to remove the skills from: claude or agents. Both when left out.`, validated the same way.

  An `--agent` value outside the set is core's usage error for that input, with exit 2. `--directory` without `--project` is an `InputError` the action throws, `Option "--directory" needs --project. Add --project, or leave out --directory.`, with exit 2. `--force` with `--project` has no effect, because a project install always replaces. No child declares a result. A root that declares arguments cannot hold children, so such an application cannot install the plugin, and an application installs it once, because a second `skills` collides under [Plugin Commands](#plugin-commands).
- **Agent targets.** `claude` and `agents`, in that order, which every child follows. A child with no `--agent` acts on both.

  | Target | Global folder | Project folder |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | `claude` | `<claude>/skills/<name>/`, where `<claude>` is `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` when it is an absolute path, else `<home>/.claude` | `<root>/.claude/skills/<name>/` |
  | `agents` | `<home>/.agents/skills/<name>/` | `<root>/.agents/skills/<name>/` |

  `<home>` is `HOME`, read from `host.env`, on every platform.
- **File modes.** Each file is written with mode `755` when `executable` is true and `644` otherwise, whatever the umask, at both scopes. Folders are created with the process's default mode.
- **Any build.** Every child acts from a `source`, `development`, or `distributed` build alike, because a skill does not depend on the binary's path.

#### Global installs

- **Checks first.** At global scope, `install`, `update`, and `uninstall` check, in this order, before they load files or read the record, and fail with a `FatalError` and exit 1 at the first that fails. `<home>`, unless every selected target is `claude` and `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` is absolute: `notes cannot find your home folder because HOME is not an absolute path. Set HOME to an absolute path, then run the command again.`, naming `USERPROFILE` on `win32`. Then the record's directory, `applicationDirectory('installation', name, host)`, which answering `{ variable }` fails: `notes cannot find its installation record because XDG_STATE_HOME is not an absolute path. Set XDG_STATE_HOME to an absolute path, then run the command again.`, naming the variable the lookup answers.
- **The record.** Each target's skill folders are recorded as installed folders in its own plugin's file in the record's directory, `skills.claude.json` and `skills.agents.json`, through the module [Installed files](#installed-files) defines, under its rules, so an install into one target never removes the other's folders. The record says which folders the plugin owns; it keeps no digest of what is inside them. Before it writes, a child reads each selected target's plugin's file through the module, and one that is damaged or holds an unknown `format` fails with `<record> cannot be read, so notes will not change the folders it lists. Remove it and the folders it lists, then run notes skills install again.`, with `uninstall` in place of `install` for that child.
- **A folder is replaced whole.** A skill folder is the unit every global child acts on. A recorded folder is replaced or removed whole, whatever someone changed, added, or removed inside it, so a new version may restructure its skill freely and an operator's edits do not survive an update. Whatever is at a folder's path is never read through: a symbolic link there is removed, never what it points to, and a link among the path's parent directories is followed.
- **One folder for both targets.** Before it reads the record, a child resolves each selected target's skills directory, `<claude>/skills` and `<home>/.agents/skills`, to its real path through the nearest ancestor that exists, so a link such as `~/.claude/skills` pointing at `~/.agents/skills` is seen. When both resolve to one directory, the child acts on the first selected target alone, records the folders there, and prints `<agents> is the same folder as <claude>, so notes acts on it once, for claude.` through `out.info`, naming the two skills directories as configured. An explicit `--agent agents` acts on it for agents, where a folder the claude record owns refuses as one the record does not list.
- **Folders the record does not list.** For `install` and `update`, anything at a skill folder's path that the target's plugin's file does not record, a directory, a symbolic link, or any other file, refuses. Both check every selected target before they write any, so a refusal writes nothing to any target. The child prints one line for each refused folder through `out.warn`, `<folder> was not installed by notes skills install.`, then fails: `notes skills install changed nothing, because folders it did not install are in the way.`, corrected by `Remove them, or run notes skills install --force to replace them.` `update` uses `notes skills update` in the failure sentence and the same correction. Under `install --force`, nothing refuses: the module replaces what is there and records the folder, and the child prints `Replaced <folder>, which notes skills install did not install.` through `out.info`.
- **Unchanged.** A skill is unchanged at a target when its folder is recorded, is a directory, and holds exactly the skill's files, no other file or folder, each with its content and the mode its `executable` names, read without following a symbolic link inside it. A target whose skills are all unchanged, and whose plugin's file records no other folder, is not written, and each of its skills prints `<folder> is unchanged.`
- **`install`.** Every selected target that is not unchanged is installed through the module with every skill's folder and files listed, in the force mode when `--force` is given. Each listed folder is written whole, and each recorded folder the install no longer lists, a skill the application stopped declaring, is removed whole. Each skill prints `Installed <name> for <target> in <folder>.`, and each removed folder prints `Removed <folder>.`
- **`update`.** It acts on each target whose plugin's file records at least one folder, as `install` with no `--force` would, and prints `Updated <name> for <target> in <folder>.` in place of the installed line. It never touches a project folder. With no target recording a folder, it prints `notes has no skills installed in your home folder, so there is nothing to update. Run notes skills install to install them.` and exits 0.
- **`uninstall`.** For each selected target, the module removes every recorded folder whole, a symbolic link there by removing the link alone, then each parent directory it created that is then empty, and deletes the plugin's file. Each removed folder prints `Removed <folder>.`, and a recorded folder already gone prints `<folder> was already gone.` through `out.info`. With no selected target recording a folder, it prints `notes has no skills installed in your home folder, so there is nothing to remove.` and exits 0. A folder the record does not list is never removed.

#### Project installs

- **The root.** `--project` starts at `host.cwd`, or at `--directory` resolved against it, and walks up through each parent to the first directory that holds an entry named `.git` of any kind, a directory in a clone and a file in a worktree or submodule. That directory is the root; with none up to the file system's root, the start is the root. A `--directory` that is not a directory fails with an `InputError` and exit 2: `Option "--directory" names /home/me/src/missing, which is not a directory. Name a directory that exists.` Both checks come before loading.
- **Never the global folder.** When a skill's project folder is that target's global folder, as when the root is the home folder, the install fails with a `FatalError` and exit 1 before it loads or writes anything: `notes skills install --project would write to /home/me/.claude/skills/notes, the folder notes skills install keeps for your home folder. Run it inside a repository, name one with --directory, or leave out --project.` The global folder is computed as Agent targets states, and both folders are resolved to their real paths through the nearest ancestor that exists before they are compared, so a project folder that reaches the global folder through a linked root, a linked `.claude` or `.agents`, or a linked home refuses too.
- **Replacing.** For each selected target and each skill, the plugin replaces whatever is at the skill's project folder, a directory with everything in it, removing each symbolic link inside it as a link and never following one, a symbolic link by removing the link alone, or any other file, with the skill's folder, written whole through a staging folder and renames as [Installed files](#installed-files) writes an installed folder. Nothing is recorded, so a project folder has no update, uninstall, or `--force`; its repository's history shows what changed. Each skill prints `Installed <name> for <target> in <folder>.`, or `Installed <name> for <target> in <folder>, replacing the copy that was there.` when something was at the folder.
- **A failed write.** A file system call that fails throws the runtime's error, which fails the run through the ordinary failure path, and the staging folder is removed. A failure between moving the old folder aside and renaming the new one into place can leave no folder and a leftover beside it; the next project install of that skill removes the leftovers of the skill's own name, as Installed files names them, and writes the folder whole.

#### Refreshing after a self-update

`refreshSkills` is an `afterReplace` function for the [self-update plugin](#self-update), which passes it a context that holds every member `RefreshContext` names. It runs in the replaced process, which holds the old version's skills, so it runs the new binary, and `update` decides what to refresh:

- **The child.** It runs `path` with the words `skills update` as a child process, with `host.env` as its environment and `host.cwd` as its working directory, no shell, no input, and its standard output and standard error piped into `host.stdout` and `host.stderr`, so the child reads neither as a terminal. It adds no time limit; the run signal ends the child with `SIGTERM`.
- **Never a failure.** A child that exits with any code but 0, or that cannot be started, adds a `warn` [log event](#logging), `Skills were not refreshed after the update.`, with the fields `path` and `code`, or `error` for a child that cannot start, and `refreshSkills` resolves. The child's own failure sentence, which says what to do, has already reached `host.stderr`. A child that cannot be started writes none, so `refreshSkills` writes one line to `host.stderr` itself: `The skills were not refreshed because /home/me/.local/bin/notes could not start. Run notes skills update.`, with the path passed through `escapeControlCharacters` and the program named by the path's last segment. A child ended by the run signal resolves the same way, and the run resolves its cancellation code under [Signals and cancellation](#signals-and-cancellation).

- **Composing.** An application that runs more after a replace calls `refreshSkills(context)` from its own `afterReplace` and awaits it. With nothing recorded, the child prints `update`'s nothing-to-update line, which names the install Command.
- **Output.** The per-skill `Installed` and `Updated` lines and the nothing-to lines go through `out.success`; the `is unchanged`, `Replaced`, `Removed`, and `already gone` lines through `out.info`; and the refused-folder lines through `out.warn`, so stdout stays empty for every child. The examples above omit the glyph each lane view adds. Every path, folder, and name a sentence repeats passes through `escapeControlCharacters`. Every refusal and check failure above is a `FatalError` that exits 1, the option conflicts are the `InputError`s above, and a throwing loader takes the ordinary failure path.
- **Names.** `skills`, `refreshSkills`, `SkillsSettings`, `Skill`, `SkillFile`, and `RefreshContext` are exported from `@loomcli/plugins/skills`.

#### Skills acceptance

The plugin is proven when process tests under Node and Bun produce these results. Each fixture sets `HOME`, `XDG_STATE_HOME`, and the working directory to temporary directories, clears `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` unless a case sets it, and runs an application that installs `skills()` with fixture skills through `run({ host })`:

- **Installing globally.** `skills install` writes every skill's folder to both global folders with the pinned modes under umask `002` and `077`, records each target's folders in its own plugin's file, and prints the pinned lines. `--agent claude` writes only the Claude folder and leaves `skills.agents.json` and its folders as they were. A second install prints the unchanged lines and writes nothing, and one after a file's mode changed, after the skill flips a file's `executable`, or after someone added a file to the folder, replaces the folder whole. An absolute `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` moves the Claude folder under it, a relative one is ignored, and `--agent claude` with an absolute `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` installs under a relative `HOME` on Linux when `XDG_STATE_HOME` is absolute. An `--agent` value outside the set exits 2.
- **Refusing.** An unrecorded directory, a regular file, and a symbolic link at a skill folder's path each fail `install` and `update` with exit 1, print the refused-folder line, and leave both targets byte for byte, including the target that had nothing in the way. A damaged and an unknown-format plugin's file each fail `install` and `uninstall` with the pinned sentence for that child. A relative `HOME` fails every global child, and a relative `XDG_STATE_HOME` with a relative `HOME` fails with the record sentence naming the variable the lookup answers.
- **Forcing.** `install --force` over an unrecorded directory, a regular file, and a symbolic link to the other target's folder, as `npx skills` leaves it, replaces each with the skill's folder, records it, prints the replaced line, and leaves the link's target byte for byte. `--force --project` installs as `--project` does.
- **Updating.** After the fixture's skill drops a reference, moves another into a subfolder, and adds a third, `update` leaves exactly the new files in the folder, including over a folder someone edited and added files to, and prints the updated lines. After the application stops declaring a skill, `update` removes that skill's folder whole. With nothing recorded it prints the nothing-to-update line and exits 0. It leaves a project folder byte for byte.
- **Uninstalling.** `uninstall` removes every recorded folder whole, including one someone edited, and each parent directory it created that is then empty, deletes the plugin's file, leaves an unrecorded folder in place, and prints the nothing-to-remove line on a second run. A recorded folder already gone prints the already-gone line. A recorded Claude folder that is now a symbolic link to the agents folder is removed as a link, and the agents folder and the link's target stay byte for byte. `--agent agents` leaves the Claude folder and its record alone. With `~/.claude/skills` a symbolic link to `~/.agents/skills`, `install` writes the folder once, records it for claude alone, prints the same-folder line, and exits 0, and `uninstall` removes it once. `uninstall` with a loader that throws calls no loader and succeeds.
- **Projects.** `install --project` from a subdirectory of a fixture repository writes to the root that holds `.git`, a directory or a file, and from a directory with no `.git` above it writes to the start. `-C` starts the walk at its directory, a missing directory exits 2, and `-C` without `--project` exits 2. Run from a home folder that holds `.git`, or from one with no `.git` above it, it fails with the never-the-global-folder sentence and writes nothing, and so does a repository whose `.claude` is a symbolic link to the home folder's `.claude`, leaving the global folder byte for byte. A second project install over a folder holding a symbolic link to a directory outside it removes the link and leaves that directory byte for byte. A second install removes a file the skill no longer lists and a file someone added, replaces a symbolic link at the folder without touching its target, and prints the replacing line. Nothing is written to the installation record.
- **Loading.** A run of any Command outside `skills` calls no loader. Each loader fault throws its pinned diagnostic when a child runs and writes nothing, and a loader that throws exits 1.
- **Refreshing.** `refreshSkills`, given a fixture binary path, runs it with `skills update`, pipes its output into the host's streams, and resolves; a child that exits 1, and a path that cannot start, each add the pinned `warn` log event and resolve, and the path that cannot start writes the pinned line to `host.stderr`. A run aborted while the child runs ends it with `SIGTERM`, and `refreshSkills` resolves. Installed as `selfUpdate({ afterReplace: refreshSkills })` under the self-update fixture, an update refreshes a recorded skill to the replaced binary's version.
- **Settings.** Each settings fault throws its pinned diagnostic at the call.
- **Packaging.** `pnpm check:packed` resolves `@loomcli/plugins/skills` from the packed tarball under Node and Bun.

### Interaction plugin

```ts
import { Application } from '@loomcli/core';
import { interaction } from '@loomcli/plugins/interaction';

const app = new Application('mimir', { plugins: [interaction({ env: 'MIMIR_INPUT' })] });
```

`@loomcli/plugins/interaction` gives an application the switch that turns its [interaction decision](#interaction) off. `interaction(settings?)` declares one global Boolean option, `input`, with `polarity: 'negative'`, so the operator types `--no-input`, the description `Ask no questions, and take every answer from options.`, `control: true`, and the [mark](#interaction) `interaction: true`. It adds no middleware, no Command, no view, and no hook, and it claims no slot. A `required: 'non-interactive'` option and a [question](prompts.md) read the decision whether or not the plugin is installed; the plugin only gives the operator the spelling.

- **`env`.** The optional setting binds one variable name or a list, under the rules of [Input sources](#input-sources), so the configuration source and the environment can turn interaction off too. The variable states the option's value, so `MIMIR_INPUT=false` turns interaction off. Core derives no name, and the plugin adds none.
- **Another spelling.** An application that wants another spelling, or a positive option, leaves the plugin out and marks its own Boolean global option. Installing the plugin beside another marked option is the two-marks declaration error.
- **Faults.** The typed settings reject a value of the wrong shape, and the factory judges none, under [Plugin settings](#plugin-settings).

#### Interaction plugin acceptance

- `mimir --help` lists `--no-input` with its description among the global options, the manifest marks it `control` and `interaction`, and `mimir setup --no-input` with stdin and stderr terminals runs with `interactive` false.
- `MIMIR_INPUT=false`, and the configuration source's `false`, turn interaction off, `MIMIR_INPUT=yes` fails with the environment grammar's usage failure, and an application that marks its own option and installs the plugin fails with the two-marks error.

### Color plugin

```ts
import { Application } from '@loomcli/core';
import { color } from '@loomcli/plugins/color';

const app = new Application('jsonkit', { plugins: [color()] });
```

`@loomcli/plugins/color` gives the operator the standard pair that sets the run's [color choice](#color). `color()` declares one global Boolean option, `color`, with `polarity: 'both'`, so the operator types `--color` or `--no-color`, the description `Turn color on or off, overriding NO_COLOR.`, `control: true`, and the [mark](#color) `color: true`. It adds no middleware, no Command, no view, and no hook, and it claims no slot. Core reads the choice and applies it; the plugin only gives the operator the spellings.

- **No settings.** `color()` declares no parameter, as `help()` and `mcp()` do, so TypeScript rejects an argument and the factory reads none. The mark rejects the two keys a setting could carry, a short alias and an `env` binding, and the pair's spelling is the standard's, so there is nothing to set.
- **Its readers.** Help lists `--[no-]color` with its description among the global options, as it lists any Boolean option of `both` polarity. The [manifest](#manifest) marks it `control` and `color`, and the [MCP](#mcp) plugin leaves it out of every tool's input schema, as it leaves out every control option.
- **Another spelling.** An application that wants another spelling, such as `--colour`, or a positive or negative option alone, leaves the plugin out and marks its own Boolean global option. Installing the plugin beside another marked option is the two-marks declaration error.
- **Names.** `color` and `ColorOptions`, the type of its options record, are exported from `@loomcli/plugins/color`.

#### Color plugin acceptance

- jsonkit installs `color()` after its example plugin, and `jsonkit --help` lists `--[no-]color` with its description after `--explain` among the global options, in the pages [The help page](#the-help-page) pins. The manifest marks it `control` and `color`, and every other Boolean option node reads `color: false`.
- On a capable terminal with `FORCE_COLOR=1`, `jsonkit --help --no-color` prints the page with no color escape, and piped, `jsonkit --help --color` prints it with color escapes.
- An application that marks its own option and installs the plugin fails with the two-marks error.
- A consumer installs the packed pack, imports `@loomcli/plugins/color`, compiles against its declarations, and `pnpm check:packed` resolves the subpath from the packed tarball under Node and Bun.

### Verbose plugin

```ts
// @loomcli/plugins/verbose
import type { Plugin, PluginOptions } from '@loomcli/core';

const options = {
  verbose: {
    control: true,
    description: 'Show more detail. Repeat it for more.',
    short: 'v',
    type: 'count',
    verbose: true,
  },
  quiet: {
    control: true,
    description: 'Hide info and success messages.',
    quiet: true,
    short: 'q',
    type: 'count',
  },
} satisfies PluginOptions;
export type VerboseOptions = typeof options;
export declare function verbose(): Plugin<VerboseOptions>;
```

```ts
import { Application } from '@loomcli/core';
import { verbose } from '@loomcli/plugins/verbose';

const app = new Application('jsonkit', { plugins: [verbose()] });
// jsonkit -v keys -f doc.json writes "› Reading doc.json." on stderr and the keys on stdout.
```

`@loomcli/plugins/verbose` gives the operator the spellings that set the run's [verbosity](#verbosity). `verbose()` declares two global counted options: `verbose`, spelled `-v, --verbose`, with the description `Show more detail. Repeat it for more.` and the mark `verbose: true`, and then `quiet`, spelled `-q, --quiet`, with the description `Hide info and success messages.` and the mark `quiet: true`. Both carry `control: true`. It adds no middleware, no Command, no view, and no hook, and it claims no slot. Core settles the verbosity and applies it; the plugin only gives the operator the spellings.

- **No settings.** `verbose()` declares no parameter, as `color()` does, so TypeScript rejects an argument and the factory reads none. `-v` and `-q` are the common standard's spellings, and the marks reject an `env` binding, so there is nothing to set.
- **Its readers.** Help lists `-v, --verbose...` and `-q, --quiet` with their descriptions among the global options. A counted option ends its spellings with `...` because each occurrence adds one, and the quiet-marked option prints none, because a further `-q` adds nothing. [Completion](#completion) reads the same rule: it stops offering `--quiet` once `-q` is given and `--verbose` once `-vv` is. The [manifest](#manifest) marks `verbose` with `control` and `verbose`, and `quiet` with `control` and `quiet`, and the [MCP](#mcp) plugin leaves both out of every tool's input schema, as it leaves out every control option.
- **Another spelling.** An application that wants another spelling, such as `--loud`, or a verbose option without a quiet one, leaves the plugin out and marks its own counted global options. Installing the plugin beside another option with either mark is that mark's two-marks declaration error, and beside an option of its own named `verbose` or `quiet`, or spelled `-v` or `-q`, it is the existing key or spelling collision under [Plugin declaration errors](#plugin-declaration-errors).
- **Names.** `verbose` and `VerboseOptions`, the type of its options record, are exported from `@loomcli/plugins/verbose`.

#### Verbose plugin acceptance

- jsonkit installs `verbose()` after `color()` and declares no verbose-marked or quiet-marked option of its own, and `jsonkit --help` lists `-v, --verbose...` and `-q, --quiet` with their descriptions after `--[no-]color`, in the pages [The help page](#the-help-page) pins. The manifest marks them `control` with `verbose` and with `quiet`, and a fixture's unmarked counted option reads `false` for both.
- `jsonkit -v keys -f doc.json` and `jsonkit -vv keys -f doc.json` write the `Reading doc.json.` debug line on stderr, `jsonkit keys -f doc.json` and `jsonkit -v -q keys -f doc.json` write none, and `jsonkit -q keys -f doc.json` writes the keys on stdout and nothing on stderr. Piped, the line is `› Reading doc.json.`.
- An application that marks its own verbose option and installs the plugin fails with the two-marks error, and so does one that marks its own quiet option.
- A consumer installs the packed pack, imports `@loomcli/plugins/verbose`, compiles against its declarations, and `pnpm check:packed` resolves the subpath from the packed tarball under Node and Bun.

### Background plugin

```ts
import { Application } from '@loomcli/core';
import { background } from '@loomcli/plugins/background';
import { loomTheme } from '@loomcli/plugins/theme';

const app = new Application('notes', { plugins: [loomTheme(), background()] });
```

`@loomcli/plugins/background` gives the operator `--background`, which sets the run's [background choice](#background). `background()` declares one global string option, `background`, with the description `Pick colors for this terminal background instead of detecting it.`, the validator `z.enum(['dark', 'light'], { error: 'Supply dark or light.' })`, `control: true`, and the [mark](#background) `background: true`. It adds no middleware, no Command, no view, and no hook, and it claims no slot. Core reads the choice and settles the background; the plugin gives the operator the spelling, and its mark makes core [detect](#background) the background even when no theme entry is adaptive, so an application whose own code reads the background installs it.

- **No settings.** `background()` declares no parameter, as `color()` does, so TypeScript rejects an argument and the factory reads none. The mark rejects the keys a setting could carry, a short alias and an `env` binding, so there is nothing to set.
- **Its readers.** Help lists `--background <background>` among the global options with its description and `One of: dark, light.`, which [Accepted values](#accepted-values) derives from the validator's schema, and [completion](#completion) offers both values. The [manifest](#manifest) marks it `control` and `background` and carries the schema, and the [MCP](#mcp) plugin leaves it out of every tool's input schema, as it leaves out every control option.
- **A wrong value.** `--background=blue` supplies no choice, so the run settles its background from the other sources, and validation fails it with exit 2 and the issue `Supply dark or light.`
- **Another spelling.** An application that wants another spelling leaves the plugin out and marks its own string global option. Installing the plugin beside another marked option is the two-marks declaration error.
- **Names.** `background` and `BackgroundOptions`, the type of its options record, are exported from `@loomcli/plugins/background`.

#### Background plugin acceptance

- A fixture application installs `loomTheme()` and `background()`. Its `--help` lists the `--background` row with its description and accepted values, its manifest marks the option `control` and `background` with the enum schema, and every other string option node reads `background: false`. No example application installs the plugin, so no example's help page or manifest changes.
- On a scripted light terminal, `--background=dark` prints the Loom theme's dark side and writes no query, and `--background=blue` fails with exit 2 and `Supply dark or light.`
- An application that marks its own option and installs the plugin fails with the two-marks error.
- A consumer installs the packed pack, imports `@loomcli/plugins/background`, compiles against its declarations, and `pnpm check:packed` resolves the subpath from the packed tarball under Node and Bun.

### Example coverage

The [help restyle acceptance](#help-and-version-restyle-acceptance) pins these byte comparisons with color and modifiers disabled. Separate expectations cover themed output.

The first-party increment is proven when both example applications install `help()` and `version()` from `@loomcli/plugins` through `plugins`, ahead of the example plugin so that help and version win a tie, and public APIs alone produce the pages above. The examples move the prose the pages print onto help's own descriptors: jsonkit's root and `get`, and textstat's root, carry `helpCommand` values with the `details` and `examples` the pages show, where each `command` omits the application name, and jsonkit's `--file` carries `helpInput({ placeholder: 'path' })`; the example plugin keeps its own descriptor and values, because the two are separate facts. The acceptance tests compare bytes: `jsonkit --help`, `jsonkit select --help`, and `textstat --help` print the three pages, `jsonkit get --help` prints the `get` page with its `details` and example while `path` is missing, `jsonkit select --bogus --help` prints the `select` page, `jsonkit fetch --help` prints the deprecated page and `jsonkit debug --help` the hidden one, and `jsonkit cache --help` on a nested fixture prints a group page with the children form alone and a `cache <command>` row on its parent's page. `jsonkit --version` and `jsonkit get --version` print `jsonkit v0.0.0` while the example manifests hold `0.0.0`, and an Application that omits `version` prints the same line. `jsonkit --help --version` prints help and never imports the version middleware module. Each case runs under Node and Bun, the pattern the seam's coverage set.

## Styles and rendering policy

Core exports the style helpers, rendering context, and rendering policy described below. [ADR-0027](decisions/0027-core-resolves-marked-output-and-one-theme-contribution.md) governs this seam. The named [Loom theme](#loom-theme) and [explicit color fallbacks](#explicit-color-fallbacks) are implemented under ADR-0022 and ADR-0029.

### Strings and composition

Core exports `style`, `glyph`, `pad`, `nowrap`, `splitLines`, and `escapeControlCharacters`. Style calls accept one string and return an ordinary string containing internal markup. Interpolation, concatenation, arrays, and `join()` work without a wrapper type or a conversion step. `style.adaptive` is the one member that styles no text: it builds a theme entry for each background, under [Background](#background).

```ts
import { glyph, pad, style } from '@loomcli/core';

const first = style.yellow.bold('Ready');
const second = style.bold(style.yellow('Ready'));
const status = `${style.green(glyph.success)} ${first}`;
const cell = pad(status, 24);
```

Both chaining and nesting are first-class. Chains apply from left to right. A later foreground or background replaces only that attribute; unrelated modifiers accumulate. An inner span overrides the attributes it supplies and restores its enclosing style afterward. The chain never mutates its receiver.

For a `warning` token mapped to yellow and bold, `style.warning.red(text)` is red and bold. `style.red.warning(text)` is yellow and bold. A token without a mapping leaves the surrounding style unchanged.

`style.escape(text)` returns a string that displays Loom's internal delimiters literally. Normal style calls preserve markup rather than escaping it. `String(value)` performs coercion and does not escape markup. The escape helper does not remove ANSI sequences; rendering policy governs them.

`escapeControlCharacters(text)` returns the text with every control character and line separator, U+0000 through U+001F, U+007F through U+009F, U+2028, and U+2029, and every bidirectional control and mark, U+202A through U+202E, U+2066 through U+2069, U+200E, U+200F, and U+061C, replaced by its four-digit lowercase `\uXXXX` escape, so raw text stays on one line, writes no control character, and cannot reorder the rest of the line. Other format characters, such as a zero-width joiner or a soft hyphen, pass through. Results output never passes through it, under rule 5 of [Failure messages](failure-messages.md#5-escape-everything-repeated). It escapes no markup, so text a view styles passes through `style.escape` as well. Core writes the reason of a broken failure view or `onFailure` hook through it, and every token, option spelling, short group, and issue path its failure sentences quote, while the failure's public fields keep the raw values. The [configuration plugin](#configuration) writes a file path through it.

First-party views escape raw data they interpolate, such as a filename taken from a data object. A string supplied to an `out.*` message method is already authored text and can contain deliberate styles. Lane views preserve that text, including its markup. Escaping a complete message would break ordinary composition.

The [wire contract](style-wire.md) fixes the delimiters, framing, literal-data rules, and malformed-input behavior. The wire form is internal and is not a persistent interchange format.

### Default styles and custom colors

The foreground catalog has all sixteen terminal colors:

| Base | Bright |
| --- | --- |
| `black` | `brightBlack` |
| `red` | `brightRed` |
| `green` | `brightGreen` |
| `yellow` | `brightYellow` |
| `blue` | `brightBlue` |
| `magenta` | `brightMagenta` |
| `cyan` | `brightCyan` |
| `white` | `brightWhite` |

Every foreground has a background counterpart: `bgBlack` through `bgWhite`, and `bgBrightBlack` through `bgBrightWhite`. Terminal palette settings determine the actual appearance of these named colors. Loom's own views do not paint backgrounds; SDK authors can use them.

The modifier catalog is `bold`, `faint`, `italic`, `underline`, `inverse`, `hidden`, `strikethrough`, and `overline`. There is no blink helper. `faint` is a terminal modifier; `dim` is a semantic theme token.

Custom colors return the same callable chain:

```ts
style.hex('#C97B36').bold('Ready');
style.rgb(201, 123, 54)('Ready');
style.ansi256(172)('Ready');
style.bgHex('#123').white('Ready');
style.bgRgb(17, 34, 51)('Ready');
style.bgAnsi256(17)('Ready');
```

Hex strings use `#RGB` or `#RRGGBB`, case-insensitively. RGB channels and ANSI palette indices are integers from 0 through 255. Alpha channels, clamping, and rounding are not supported. Invalid arguments throw when the helper is called, before a marked string is produced. Helpers do not coerce non-string text or invalid numeric input.

Three scoped resets are chainable:

| Helper | Effect inside its span |
| --- | --- |
| `reset` | Clear foreground, background, and modifiers |
| `resetForeground` | Use the terminal's foreground default; retain other attributes |
| `resetBackground` | Use the terminal's background default; retain other attributes |

`style.reset.red(text)` clears inherited styling and then applies red. Closing the span restores the enclosing style. A token mapped to `style.reset` explicitly clears inherited styling. An omitted mapping does not clear anything.

### Explicit color fallbacks

```ts
import type { Style } from '@loomcli/core';

export type ColorName =
	| 'black' | 'red' | 'green' | 'yellow' | 'blue' | 'magenta' | 'cyan' | 'white'
	| 'brightBlack' | 'brightRed' | 'brightGreen' | 'brightYellow'
	| 'brightBlue' | 'brightMagenta' | 'brightCyan' | 'brightWhite';

export interface ColorFallbacks {
	readonly ansi256?: number | undefined;
	readonly ansi16?: ColorName | undefined;
}

export type Ansi256Fallbacks = Pick<ColorFallbacks, 'ansi16'>;

// These members extend the existing Style type.
interface ColorHelpers<Names extends string, Semantic extends boolean> {
	hex(color: string, fallbacks?: ColorFallbacks): Style<Names, Semantic>;
	rgb(red: number, green: number, blue: number, fallbacks?: ColorFallbacks): Style<Names, Semantic>;
	ansi256(index: number, fallbacks?: Ansi256Fallbacks): Style<Names, Semantic>;
	bgHex(color: string, fallbacks?: ColorFallbacks): Style<Names, Semantic>;
	bgRgb(red: number, green: number, blue: number, fallbacks?: ColorFallbacks): Style<Names, Semantic>;
	bgAnsi256(index: number, fallbacks?: Ansi256Fallbacks): Style<Names, Semantic>;
}
```

```ts
const sage = style.hex('#7A8F7B', { ansi256: 108, ansi16: 'green' });
const rgbSage = style.rgb(122, 143, 123, { ansi256: 108, ansi16: 'green' });
const indexedSage = style.ansi256(108, { ansi16: 'green' });
sage.bold('Ready');
```

- **Status.** These helper extensions and the three types exported by core are implemented under [ADR-0029](decisions/0029-explicit-color-fallbacks-preserve-theme-hues.md).
- **Selection.** RGB and hex retain their original RGB value at truecolor depth. At 256 or 16 colors, the matching explicit fallback wins. An omitted or `undefined` fallback uses the existing approximation of the original color for that depth. A 256-color fallback never changes the 16-color result. `ansi256` retains its original index at truecolor and 256-color depth, and uses `ansi16` when supplied at 16-color depth.
- **Values.** `ansi256` is an integer from 0 through 255. `ansi16` is one of the sixteen foreground color names, including for background helpers. Both options are optional. `undefined` options and an empty object behave as omission. The `ansi256` and `bgAnsi256` helpers accept only `ansi16`.
- **Validation.** Helpers validate options when called and copy the accepted values into the chain. Later object mutation cannot change that chain. A non-plain options object, unknown option, or invalid color name throws `TypeError`. An invalid palette index throws `RangeError`. Existing hex and RGB validation remains unchanged. No value is coerced, rounded, or clamped.
- **Composition.** Fallbacks belong to one color operation. A later foreground replaces the original foreground and all its fallbacks, so `sage.blue` uses named blue at every depth. A background operation leaves the foreground choice intact. Nesting and embedded ANSI resets restore enclosing colors with their fallbacks. All helpers retain the receiver's token names and semantic-chain restriction.
- **Callbacks.** Helpers accept only their documented arguments. A callback such as `values.map(style.hex)` passes the array index as the options argument and now fails validation. Use `values.map((value) => style.hex(value))` so the helper receives only the color.
- **Policy.** Fallbacks do not change capability detection or force color. Color suppression removes them like other colors. Direct styles and theme mappings use the same rules. Calls that omit the options argument preserve their current behavior. Named terminal colors and raw ANSI colors gain no inferred fallback mapping.

#### Fallback acceptance

The implementation verifies exact bytes for explicit and omitted fallbacks at all three depths, including `ansi256` source colors and background helpers. It verifies that an index passed by a direct array callback is rejected and an explicit one-argument wrapper succeeds. It covers partial and `undefined` options, invalid options at helper-call time, copied option values, whole-color replacement, nested restoration, embedded resets, and color suppression. Type checks reject invalid fields and names while preserving chain typing. The wire checks validate the new color forms and retain the existing forms, as specified in the [wire contract](style-wire.md#explicit-color-fallbacks). Node and Bun process fixtures plus packed consumers prove the public API.

### Theme plugins and typed names

The core semantic names are `dim`, `primary`, `highlight`, `success`, `warning`, `error`, and `info`. These are names, not built-in appearances.

The plugin pack exports the bare `theme(mapping)` factory from `@loomcli/plugins/theme`:

```ts
import { Application, style } from '@loomcli/core';
import { theme } from '@loomcli/plugins/theme';

const app = new Application('example', {
	plugins: [
		theme({
			highlight: style.yellow.bold,
			identifier: style.cyan,
		}),
	],
});
```

`theme(mapping)` supplies exactly the mappings provided. Its plugin identity is `@loomcli/plugins/theme`. Importing it installs nothing.

The [`loomTheme(overrides?)`](#loom-theme) factory adds the named palette and accepts replacements and custom keys.

#### `PluginDefinition.theme` field

A [PluginDefinition](#plugins) can contribute this field:

| Field | Required | Value |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `theme` | No | A readonly mapping from semantic names to unapplied concrete style chains, [adaptive styles](#background), or `undefined`, retaining its literal keys through the returned plugin type. |

Supplying the field claims the theme slot, including an empty mapping. The pack factory uses this field; third-party themes use their own plugin identities:

```ts
import { plugin, style } from '@loomcli/core';

export const dusk = () => plugin('@example/dusk', {
	theme: {
		highlight: style.magenta.bold,
		identifier: style.cyan,
	},
});
```

The contribution retains its literal keys in the returned plugin type and through Application installation. A broad annotation must not erase the vocabulary along the framework's internal path. Theme declarations require no middleware and perform no output or capability detection during construction. They follow the same mapping validation and single-owner rule as the pack factories.

One Application installs at most one theme plugin. A second claim on the theme slot is a `DeclarationError` under `@loomcli/core/slot-taken` from the Application constructor that names both claimants and marks both entries of `plugins`. Zero themes is valid. Without a mapping, semantic tokens inherit their enclosing style; direct colors and modifiers still work under rendering policy.

In a bare theme, an omitted or undefined mapping contributes no style. An explicitly declared custom key with an undefined value still introduces that name.

Mapping values are unapplied concrete style chains: named terminal colors, modifiers, resets, custom colors, or their combinations. A value may instead be an [adaptive style](#background), `style.adaptive({ dark, light })`, whose two sides are such chains and which core resolves against the run's background. A mapping cannot reference any semantic token, including a core token. For example, `highlight: style.info.bold` fails the type contract. Shared concrete chain constants are valid. The types reject a name a built-in style member holds. A mapping value that is neither an unapplied concrete chain nor an adaptive style throws a plain `TypeError` from `plugin()`, because core finds no style operations for it.

The mapping's custom keys introduce one flat semantic vocabulary for the Application. The same key always names the same token within that Application. There are no public token descriptors, style groups, per-view namespaces, or group override methods. A custom key cannot shadow a built-in style member, including callable-function members. Core semantic keys are valid mapping keys because they configure those tokens.

The Application derives this vocabulary from its installed theme and publishes it through one Application-owned type registration. Independently authored Commands, extracted action handlers, and `View<Data>` values receive those names automatically. A misspelled name fails compilation. There is no per-Command theme argument, manual token generic, or Application-owned Command factory.

Custom names use automatic Application environment registration. It registers a shallow configuration type rather than a completed command tree, avoiding a circular dependency through handlers. One compilation context has one default registration; reusable libraries express their requirements without registering a consumer's Application. ADR-0026 supplies this registration API and its compatibility checks. Style derives custom names from the installed plugins in that environment, including when ordinary plugins accompany the theme.

Core supplies `style` on the action context and in the second view-function argument. The imported `style` supplies concrete styles and core semantic names; theme authoring needs no Application instance.

Actions use the supplied `style` to access the installed theme's custom names. Pass that style to helpers that compose action output.

```ts
import { Command } from '@loomcli/core';

export const show = new Command('show')
	.argument('name', { required: true })
	.action(({ args, out, style }) => out.print(style.identifier(style.escape(args.name))));
```

This action belongs to the Application compilation context that declares `identifier`, as does the view below.

```ts
import type { View } from '@loomcli/core';

interface Item {
	name: string;
}

export const item: View<Item> = {
	render: (data, { style, width }) => {
		const text = style.identifier(style.escape(data.name));
		return `${text} (${width(text)} columns)\n`;
	},
};
```

This example belongs to the Application compilation context that declares `identifier`. The view context is immutable and supplies `style`, destination-aware `width(text)`, `plain(text)`, `columns`, `wrap(text, columns)`, `expandTabs(text)`, and the run's [`background`](#background). Existing one-argument view functions can ignore it. A view remains pure and synchronous and receives no output handle. Under `out.render`, as here, it owns its trailing newline; a lane view returns none, as [Rendered output](#rendered-output) states per write site. Core resolves its returned markup and ANSI policy before writing, so returned strings no longer promise exact output bytes.

### Glyphs

`glyph` contains the complete [glyph catalog](glyphs.md), derived from a pinned Inquirer figures inventory. Each property is an unstyled marked string. `success` aliases `tick`, and `error` aliases `cross`; `info` and `warning` retain the upstream names. A glyph carries no theme token or automatic color.

```ts
style.success(glyph.success);
style.cyan(glyph.success);
glyph.success;
```

The first two expressions style the glyph explicitly; the last inherits its surroundings. The inventory preserves upstream compatibility forms, which can contain Unicode or multiple characters. There is no separate strict ASCII mode. For example, `tick` selects `✔` or `√`, `cross` selects `✘` or `×`, and `radioOn` selects `◉` or `(*)`.

Core applies the pinned Inquirer detection rule to captured facts on each run. On every platform, main forms apply unless `TERM` is `linux`, where core selects compatibility forms. Inquirer's separate Windows rule is not applied, under [ADR-0100](decisions/0100-acceptance-plans-live-beside-the-tests.md). It reads the captured environment case-sensitively. Piping, `NO_COLOR`, `FORCE_COLOR`, and theme installation do not select glyph forms. Only marked glyphs participate; core does not search and replace arbitrary Unicode characters in data.

### Rendering policies

Both Application options and `run()` options accept `rendering`:

```ts
const app = new Application('example', {
	rendering: {
		color: 'auto',
		modifiers: 'auto',
		hyperlinks: 'auto',
		terminalControls: 'strip',
		background: 'auto',
	},
});

await app.run({ rendering: { color: 'never' } });
```

`color`, `modifiers`, and `hyperlinks` each accept `'auto'`, `'always'`, or `'never'`. Their default is `'auto'`. `terminalControls` accepts `'strip'` or `'preserve'`, defaulting to `'strip'`. `background` accepts `'auto'`, `'dark'`, or `'light'`, defaulting to `'auto'`: `'dark'` and `'light'` state the run's [background](#background) over every source but the operator's background choice, except in an invocation by name, which settles nothing and reads `undefined`, and `'auto'` leaves it to the sources after the author's. Undefined fields act as omitted fields. Invalid values are declaration errors and name the field and accepted values.

There is one policy for both streams. No field accepts a stdout/stderr map. Core evaluates automatic capabilities separately for each destination. Redirecting stdout therefore does not turn off capable stderr output.

Invocation overrides replace only supplied rendering fields. Omitted fields retain the Application setting. Explicit `'auto'` restores automatic behavior for that field. This merge applies to rendering policy alone: `host` overrides still replace whole fields under [ADR-0009](decisions/0009-core-captures-the-host-and-resolves-an-exit-code.md).

The operator's [color choice](#color), `--color` or `--no-color` on an Application that declares the color mark, comes first for the `color` field alone: it sets `'always'` or `'never'` over the merged policy and over both variables, and every other field keeps its own policy. Without a choice, explicit `'always'` or `'never'` wins for its policy. With color set to `'auto'`, precedence is nonempty `FORCE_COLOR`, nonempty `NO_COLOR`, then terminal detection. Empty values make no override. The string `"0"` is nonempty and therefore active for either variable. A nonempty `FORCE_COLOR` wins when both variables are active. Numeric values do not select a color depth.

These rules follow [NO_COLOR](https://no-color.org/) and [FORCE_COLOR](https://force-color.org/), including user configuration precedence and the standard's rule that an argument given for one run overrides `NO_COLOR`, which the [color choice](#color) implements. They deliberately differ from Node's numeric `FORCE_COLOR` interpretation. Core owns the behavior under both Node and Bun.

| Automatic case | Colors | Modifiers | Hyperlinks |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Capable TTY | On | On | Preserve |
| Capable TTY with `NO_COLOR` | Off | On | Preserve |
| Pipe or file | Off | Off | Strip, retaining visible text |
| Pipe or file with `FORCE_COLOR` | On | On | Strip, retaining visible text |

For ANSI color and modifier detection, a capable TTY has `isTTY: true` and `TERM` other than `dumb`. Automatic modifiers follow that detection or a nonempty `FORCE_COLOR`; `NO_COLOR` never disables them. Automatic hyperlinks require `isTTY: true`. Explicit policy values override each column independently. Setting color to `'always'` alone does not change the modifier or hyperlink policy.

When colors are enabled, core determines depth on each emission from the hints the run's environment holds, a variable [environment preparation](#environment-preparation) imported included, in this order:

| Hint | Depth |
| --- | --- |
| `COLORTERM` is `truecolor` or `24bit` | Truecolor |
| `TERM` is `xterm-kitty`, `xterm-ghostty`, or `wezterm` | Truecolor |
| `TERM_PROGRAM` is `iTerm.app` and its version starts with a decimal major of at least 3 | Truecolor |
| `TERM_PROGRAM` is `iTerm.app` otherwise | 256 |
| `TERM_PROGRAM` is `Apple_Terminal` | 256 |
| `TERM` ends in `-256` or `-256color`, case-insensitively | 256 |
| No matching hint | 16 |

The iTerm version field is `TERM_PROGRAM_VERSION`. These are a portable subset of [supports-color's detection rules](https://github.com/chalk/supports-color/blob/e2a4cd3c44eb384b075161ef32859cd29ce1aa7f/index.js), with enablement handled separately. Core does not read CLI flags or live process globals during resolution, and does not reuse upstream numeric forcing semantics. The [color choice](#color) reads `host.argv` once, before resolution, for the marked option's spellings alone, unlike supports-color's scan of `process.argv`, and the [background choice](#background) reads it once beside it for its own marked option. Forced color without a depth hint uses sixteen colors. A future detector update needs equivalent Node and Bun evidence.

[Explicit fallbacks](#explicit-color-fallbacks) take precedence at their named depth. Without a matching fallback, the following approximation rule applies.

RGB colors remain RGB at truecolor depth. At lower depth, core chooses the closest available color by squared RGB distance, with the lower palette index breaking ties. The 256-color target is the conventional xterm palette. The sixteen-color target uses that palette's first sixteen entries. Named colors retain their terminal palette indices; they do not acquire hard-coded RGB values on a richer terminal. ANSI-256 colors retain their index at 256 or truecolor depth and approximate to sixteen colors at basic depth. A terminal can customize its palette, so approximation does not promise an exact visual match.

The same policies apply to ANSI styling already embedded in supplied strings. Color suppression removes foreground and background colors, not unrelated modifiers or text. An embedded reset restores the enclosing Loom style. Core closes remaining style and hyperlink state at the end of each rendered string.

General terminal controls include cursor movement, screen erasure, title changes, and the bell. The default removes those commands while retaining ordinary text, tabs, and line breaks. `'preserve'` permits them without bypassing color, modifier, or hyperlink policy. OSC 8 hyperlinks have their own policy even though their encoding uses terminal control sequences. Disabling hyperlinks preserves the label exactly and does not append the destination URL. No hyperlink authoring helper is added by this contract.

For filtered control strings such as OSC, core removes the complete sequence through its terminator, including its payload. An unterminated control string is removed through the end of the rendered string. When controls are preserved, complete unrecognized controls pass through; recognized styling and hyperlinks still obey their own policies. The resolver must not misclassify a control-string payload as ordinary text or as another output command.

Core discards an incomplete ANSI sequence at the end of each rendered string, including in preserve mode. Commands cannot span separate output calls. For example, separate view results containing `ESC[3` and `1mX` emit only the literal `1mX`, not a red-color command. Within one rendered string, ANSI recognition spans adjacent Loom frames, as the [wire contract](style-wire.md#parsing-order) specifies.

### Width, padding, and multiline lanes

The view context also supplies `plain(text): string`, which resolves marked text without colors, modifiers, hyperlinks, or terminal controls, while keeping that destination’s glyph forms and padding. A view can clip the plain text at grapheme boundaries and escape the result before applying its own styles.

The view context supplies `width(text): number`. It resolves glyph forms for that destination, ignores styling and hyperlink envelopes, and counts Unicode terminal columns. Combining marks add no column; wide characters occupy two. Emoji sequences follow the selected Unicode width implementation. Ambiguous-width characters count as one column. Measurement and padding use the grapheme width rules of `@rockorager/uucode` 2.2.1 with its Unicode 17 data. Core carries both itself, the tables as a JavaScript module, so it reads no file at run time. The tables stay under the Unicode License v3, which core's license field and its `NOTICE` state, and their license notices are legal comments that a bundler keeps in the bundle. It does not promise identical font rendering in every terminal.

`width()` returns the widest line's width. Tabs advance to the next multiple of eight columns, starting each input line at column zero. Thus `width('a\tb')` is 9. CRLF is one line break; LF is a line break. Preserved cursor operations do not turn width measurement into a terminal emulator.

Deep padding around unchanged content reuses measurement. Nested padding that changes the content at every level can still require quadratic Unicode measurement, such as appending one combining mark per level. This pathological optimization is deferred; the [wire contract](style-wire.md#resolution) includes a reproducible probe.

The view context supplies `columns: number | undefined`, the effective width of the destination the view's text reaches. Core reads it live. Just before each render call it takes the destination's real width from `host.terminal` and passes the result to the view as a plain number, so a resize between two renders reaches the next one, and core never renders printed text again: a [live region](#live-region) redraws the frame text it kept. Each context belongs to one destination, so a view rendered to stdout reads stdout's width and a view rendered to stderr reads stderr's. Core builds a fresh context, with its own `columns`, for every render call: each lane write, `out.render`, result render, failure view, incomplete-result line, `out.draw`, each live region's `draw`, and each `head`, `row`, and `tail` of a row view. A whole view over a sequence reads the width when it renders, after the source ends. `columns` is `undefined` when that destination is not a terminal: a pipe, a redirect to a file, `app.invoke`, and so every MCP tool call. It is also `undefined` on a terminal that reports no width and whose `COLUMNS` holds no positive integer. The context carries no fallback width, because a view that read 80 for a pipe could not tell a pipe from an 80-column terminal. A view that wants a fallback supplies its own, such as `context.columns ?? 80`. `FailureViewContext` extends `ViewContext`, so failure views receive `columns`, `wrap`, and `expandTabs` too.

`COLUMNS` only narrows. It is valid when `host.env.COLUMNS` is a positive integer: ASCII digits 0-9 only, leading zeros allowed, a safe integer greater than zero. Any other value, such as `0`, `abc`, `-5`, `60.5`, `+60`, `6e1`, a value with a leading or trailing space, or an empty string, is ignored. On a terminal that reports a width, `columns` is the smaller of that width and a valid `COLUMNS`, and the real width otherwise, so `COLUMNS` never widens a layout past the screen. On a terminal that reports no width, `columns` is a valid `COLUMNS`, and `undefined` otherwise. On a destination that is not a terminal, `columns` is `undefined` whatever `COLUMNS` says, because some shells export `COLUMNS` and piped output would otherwise wrap unasked. `host.terminal.stdout.columns` and `host.terminal.stderr.columns` are the real readings and never reflect `COLUMNS`. The row count `out.draw` resolves to uses the real stderr width read at that draw.

`pad(text, minimumWidth, options?)` returns a marked string. `options.align` is `'left'`, `'right'`, or `'center'`, defaulting to `'left'`. Padding uses spaces only. It supplies a minimum width, never truncates text, and puts an odd extra space on the right for center alignment. Width arguments are nonnegative safe integers.

```ts
pad('cat', 8);
pad('cat', 8, { align: 'right' });
pad('cat', 8, { align: 'center' });
```

These produce five spaces after `cat`, five spaces before it, or two before and three after it. Core defers actual padding until glyph selection, so a compatibility form such as `(*)` occupies its real width. Padding expands tabs within each input line before adding alignment spaces. Ordinary output outside padding preserves tabs, except where a view expands them with `expandTabs`, below, as the marked lanes, the table, and the records layout do on a terminal.

Padding applies to each line independently and preserves line breaks. A trailing newline does not create a padded extra empty line. Interior blank lines are lines and receive the requested padding. For example, `pad('cat\ndog', 5)` resolves to `cat  \ndog  `, while `pad('cat\n', 5)` resolves to `cat  \n`. CRLF remains CRLF. The empty string has width zero; padding it produces the requested number of spaces.

`nowrap(text)` returns a marked string, as `pad` does. It takes one string and throws `TypeError('Style helpers require a string.')` for any other value, as `pad` does. The frame is deferred and resolves to its body exactly: it adds no byte, expands no tab itself, and measures as its body, so copying the printed text gives the exact text. A view that expands tabs with `expandTabs` expands a tab inside the frame as any other, and the frame still keeps its body whole. Frames nest, so a style or a glyph inside it is fine. It exists for line breaking: `wrap` keeps its body whole, and a table's floor counts it whole. A path that holds spaces is the case it serves.

```ts
import { nowrap } from '@loomcli/core';

out.info(`Wrote ${nowrap(path)}`);
```

With `path` set to `/Users/a/Library/Application Support/x` and a lane that leaves 30 columns for the message, the path stays on one line and the text before it wraps:

```text
ℹ Wrote
  /Users/a/Library/Application Support/x
```

The view context supplies `wrap(text, columns): string`, which breaks lines when the view runs. It measures with that destination's glyph forms exactly as `width()` does, ignores styling and hyperlink envelopes, and returns marked text with real line breaks inserted. It is not a deferred frame. `pad` stays the deferred minimum-width composer, and the [wire contract](style-wire.md) gains one frame for line breaking, `nowrap`, below. The idiom is `context.wrap(text, context.columns)`. With `columns` undefined, `wrap` returns the text unchanged, so the same view wraps at a terminal and passes the text through a pipe. Any other `columns` that is not a positive safe integer throws `RangeError('Wrap width must be a positive safe integer.')`.

- **Greedy.** Each output line takes as many words as fit within `columns`, and a line exactly `columns` wide fits.
- **Breaks are at spaces only.** The only break opportunity is U+0020. Text without spaces, such as Chinese, Japanese, or Thai prose, does not wrap, however wide it is. `wrap` implements no Unicode line-breaking rules.
- **Line breaks are kept.** LF and CRLF stay as written, CRLF stays CRLF, and each input line wraps independently. An inserted break is LF, or CRLF on an input line that ends in CRLF.
- **A long word stays whole.** A word wider than `columns` keeps a line of its own and is never split, so a URL, a token, a hash, a path without spaces, or any text inside `nowrap` copies intact.
- **Spaces at a break are dropped.** An input line's leading spaces are never a break, and they stay with its first word. Spaces at the end of an input line are never a break, and they stay with its last word. Both count toward the fit, so `wrap('ab cd   ', 5)` is `ab` and then `cd   `. Continuation lines start at column 0, and indenting them is the caller's job. Runs of spaces inside a line are kept.
- **Tabs** measure at stops of eight as `width()` does, and a line never breaks at a tab. `wrap` keeps each tab as written, so its stops count from column 0 of each output line. A view that places the wrapped text after other text expands the tabs first with `expandTabs`, below, as the marked lanes, the table, and the records layout do on a terminal.
- **A `pad` frame or a `nowrap` frame is one unit.** `wrap` measures a `pad` frame at its padded width and a `nowrap` frame at the width of its body, and never breaks inside either.
- **A style or a hyperlink that spans a break** continues across it. The break is inserted inside the envelope, as an authored line break sits, so the span continues on the next line. A lane's gutter on a continuation line carries the span as it does after an authored break.

Loom's first-party messages wrap each filesystem path and URL they print in `nowrap`, so a path that holds spaces, such as a macOS folder under `Application Support`, stays whole on screen. They do so wherever the text resolves frames: a lane, a view such as the service status view, and a `FatalError`'s message. An `InputError`'s default text prints its message as data, so a frame there would show its delimiters, and a path in an `InputError`'s message, such as the configuration plugin's `File "…"` failure, or in a wrong value's label stays unmarked. The wrapping changes no message text, because `nowrap` adds no bytes.

```ts
import type { View } from '@loomcli/core';

export const notice: View<string> = {
	render: (message, context) => `${context.wrap(message, context.columns)}\n`,
};
```

At 30 columns, `Copy the file to /srv/releases/2026-10-17/archive.tar.gz and restart the service.` renders as three lines. The path is wider than 30 columns, so it keeps the second line whole.

```text
Copy the file to
/srv/releases/2026-10-17/archive.tar.gz
and restart the service.
```

The view context supplies `expandTabs(text): string`, which replaces each tab in marked text with spaces up to the next multiple of eight columns, counted from the start of the tab's own input line as `width()` counts, so text a view places after a gutter, a label, or another column shows on screen as it measured. The terminal counts a tab's stop from the screen's column 0, so a tab left in text placed at an offset can move by up to seven columns and push the line past `columns`. `expandTabs` measures with that destination's glyph forms, as `width()` does, and keeps every frame header, escape, and ANSI command byte for byte. A tab inside a style frame or a `nowrap` frame expands as any other, and a tab inside an ANSI control string, such as an OSC payload, is no tab and stays. A tab inside a `pad` frame stays, because the frame already expands it from its own start when it resolves. The spaces a tab becomes are ordinary spaces, so `wrap` may break at them outside a `nowrap` frame. `expandTabs('a\tb')` is `a` and seven spaces before `b`, and text without a tab comes back unchanged. It is unconditional: a view that keeps tabs off a terminal calls it only when `columns` is defined, as the marked lanes, the table, and the records layout do.

There is no align helper. A caller aligns a wrapped block by pairing `wrap` with `pad`, whose alignment applies to each line: `pad(context.wrap(text, 20), 20, { align: 'center' })`.

`splitLines(text)` splits marked text at its line breaks, LF and CRLF, into an array of lines that each stand alone, for a view that places lines beside other text, as a table places a cell's lines beside the next column and the records view places a value's lines after its indent. Every frame open at a line's end, a style, a `pad` frame, or a `nowrap` frame, closes there and opens again at the start of the next line, in its nesting order. An SGR attribute and an OSC 8 hyperlink embedded in the text end at each line's end and start again on the next, so nothing on one line styles or links the text placed after it. A line that sets an SGR attribute sits in a style frame with no operation, whose end restores the style around it and adds no byte to the output. The line breaks themselves are dropped. A trailing line break ends the last line and adds no empty line, the rule `pad` follows for a trailing newline, while a blank line inside the text is a line: `splitLines('a\n')` is `['a']`, and `splitLines('a\n\nb')` is `['a', '', 'b']`. A line break inside an ANSI control string, such as an OSC payload, is not a line break. Text without a line break comes back as one line, unchanged unless it sets an SGR attribute or leaves a hyperlink open. `splitLines` breaks only where the text already has a line break, so a view pairs it with `wrap`: `splitLines(context.wrap(text, width))`. It reads the wire with the parser core's resolver uses, and takes one string, throwing `TypeError('Style helpers require a string.')` for any other value, as `pad` does.

```ts
import { splitLines, style } from '@loomcli/core';

splitLines(style.red('one\ntwo'));
// [style.red('one'), style.red('two')]
```

Lane views receive the original message string, including line breaks and authored styles. Core does not split it into a new data structure or infer that later lines are details. A lane view owns its glyph gutter and continuation indentation. It measures the selected glyph form rather than assuming one column. The built-in `info`, `success`, `warn`, and `error` lanes prefix the first line with the matching glyph and one space. The `debug` lane prefixes it with `glyph.pointerSmall` and one space, and the `trace` lane with two spaces, `glyph.lineVerticalDashed0`, and one space, so a trace line's gutter measures the glyph plus three. The `debug` lane styles its glyph and the message `dim` and the `trace` lane styles them `dim.faint`, the spaces of either gutter unstyled, and the message keeps its author's styles inside that frame. Continuation lines use spaces for that gutter without repeating the glyph. Those six lanes also wrap the message with `wrap` at `columns` minus the measured gutter, which fits the message in the columns right of the gutter, and every continuation line carries the gutter, whether the break is authored or wrapped. When `columns` is defined, before they wrap, they expand each tab in the message to spaces with `expandTabs`, counted from the start of its own line of the message, inside style and `nowrap` frames too, so the gutter moves no tab stop and lane output on a terminal holds no tab. With `columns` undefined, as on a pipe or under an invocation by name, lane output is byte for byte what it would be without wrapping, tabs included. With no column left after the gutter, the message is not wrapped, and its tabs still expand. `print` remains prefix-free and never wraps. An application that wants unwrapped lanes replaces the lane view, as it can replace any lane view. The semantic methods retain their string-only call shape and newline contract. Each lane is a declared view core exports under `lanes`, and an application replaces its function through `views` as [Views](#views) describes; the newline the semantic method appends is outside the view and survives any override.

### Implementation acceptance

The style tests and packed consumers cover these obligations:

- Chaining, nesting, each reset, no-theme inheritance, and rejection of token references in theme mappings.
- Every foreground, background, modifier, and custom-color helper, including invalid arguments and capability degradation.
- The complete pinned glyph catalog, semantic aliases, multi-character compatibility forms, and independence from themes and ANSI policy.
- Automatic custom-name inference in detached Commands and views after the registration prerequisite, with typo and reserved-name rejection.
- Every rendering-policy field, invocation override behavior, nonempty `"0"` environment values, conflicting variables, and independent destinations under one policy.
- Embedded ANSI colors and resets, separate hyperlink and terminal-control policies, and malformed control strings.
- Literal marker data, nested deferred padding, Unicode width, tabs, multiline strings, and the adversarial cases in the wire contract.
- Fresh host capture on repeated runs, no import-time capability capture, and equivalent output under Node and Bun.
- Columns per destination: a view rendered to stdout reads stdout's width and one rendered to stderr reads stderr's, when the two streams report different widths and when only one is a terminal.
- Columns without a terminal: a pipe, a redirect to a file, `app.invoke`, and an MCP tool call each read `columns` as `undefined`, with `COLUMNS=60` set as well, and `wrap` returns the text unchanged.
- Live width: under a pty-backed host, one run renders twice either side of a resize, and the first render reads 100 columns and the second 60. The first render's text is not redrawn. `host.terminal.stdout.columns` and `host.terminal.stderr.columns` read the new width after the resize, and a reported 0 reads `undefined`.
- `COLUMNS` only narrows on a terminal destination: `COLUMNS=60` over a real width of 100 gives `columns` 60, `COLUMNS=150` over 100 gives 100, and `060` over 100 gives 60. `COLUMNS` set to ` 60`, `+60`, `60 `, `6e1`, `0`, `abc`, `-5`, `60.5`, an empty string, or an integer beyond the safe range leaves 100.
- `COLUMNS` on a terminal that reports no width: it reads `COLUMNS=60` as 60 and reads `undefined` without `COLUMNS`. `COLUMNS=60` on a pipe leaves `undefined`.
- The host facts stay real: `host.terminal.stdout.columns` and `host.terminal.stderr.columns` read the real width and never reflect `COLUMNS`. A host override of plain numbers stays fixed across renders, and an override that supplies a getter is read each time. `isTTY` is captured once.
- `out.draw` resolves the row count for the real stderr width read at that draw, under `COLUMNS=60` and after a resize alike.
- Greedy fitting: each output line takes as many words as fit within `columns`, and a line exactly `columns` wide stays on one line, while a line one column wider breaks.
- Breaks at spaces only: a break only at U+0020, never at a tab, and runs of spaces inside a line kept.
- `expandTabs`: each tab becomes spaces to the next multiple of eight from the start of its input line, each line of a CRLF or LF text counted alone, measured in the destination's glyph forms, so a tab after `◉` takes seven spaces and after `(*)` five. A tab inside a style frame or a `nowrap` frame expands and the frame resolves as before, a tab inside a `pad` frame is left to the frame, and a tab inside an OSC 8 payload stays.
- Tabs in a lane: on a terminal 11 columns wide, `out.warn('aaaaaa\tb c')` prints `⚠ aaaaaa  b` and then `  c`, so no line passes 11 columns and none holds a tab, and the same holds for the message inside `nowrap` and inside a style. Off a terminal, the lane keeps the tab, and `print` keeps it everywhere.
- Line breaks: LF and CRLF kept, with each input line wrapped alone, and an inserted break is LF, or CRLF on an input line that ends in CRLF.
- Leading spaces: an input line's leading spaces are never a break and stay with its first word, so an indented path wider than `columns` keeps its indent on its own line.
- Trailing spaces: spaces at the end of an input line are never a break, stay with its last word, and count toward the fit, so `ab cd   ` at 5 columns breaks before `cd   `, and a records value or a table cell whose trailing space would pass the width wraps instead of overflowing.
- Dropped spaces: the spaces at a break are dropped, and continuation lines start at column 0.
- A word wider than `columns` stays whole on its own line, for a URL, a token, a hash, a path without spaces, and any text inside `nowrap`.
- A `pad` frame or a `nowrap` frame is one unit: `wrap` measures a `pad` frame at its padded width and a `nowrap` frame at its body's width, and never breaks inside either.
- `nowrap`: a body never breaks at any `columns`, and it resolves byte for byte to its body, so a printed `nowrap` path copies as the exact text. A lane message holding `nowrap('/Users/a/Library/Application Support/x')` at a narrow width keeps the path on one line, and the text around it wraps. A table cell in `nowrap` raises its column's floor to the whole cell. A style or a glyph inside the frame, and the frame inside a `pad` frame, resolve as without it. A non-string throws `TypeError('Style helpers require a string.')`, as `pad` does.
- First-party messages: each filesystem path and URL a first-party message prints through a lane, a view, or a `FatalError` is inside `nowrap`, the service status view's unit path included, and the message text is byte for byte what it was. A `nowrap` frame in an `InputError`'s message prints its delimiters on a pipe and on a terminal, while one in a `FatalError`'s message resolves to its body on both, so the configuration plugin's named-file failure and a wrong value's label print a path that holds spaces whole and unmarked.
- `splitLines` frames: a style, a `pad` frame, and a `nowrap` frame that span a line break close at the line's end and open again on the next line, nested frames in their order, and a frame closed before the break stays closed. A style header that names a theme token splits like any style, and an escaped delimiter or a glyph frame is text.
- `splitLines` embedded ANSI: an embedded SGR color, set at the top level, inside a style, or inside a `pad` frame, ends at each line's end and is set again on the next, and an embedded OSC 8 hyperlink closes at each line's end and opens again on the next.
- `splitLines` breaks: LF and CRLF split alike and are dropped, a trailing line break adds no empty line while a blank line inside the text stays, a `pad` frame after the last break is a line, a line break inside a control string does not split, text without a break comes back unchanged, and a non-string throws `TypeError('Style helpers require a string.')`.
- A style and a hyperlink that span a break continue across it, with the break inside the envelope as an authored line break sits, as a rendering with color and hyperlinks on shows, and a lane's gutter on a continuation line carries the span.
- Glyph measurement per destination: a message with a marked glyph whose main and compatibility forms differ in width breaks at different points for a destination that selects main forms and one that selects compatibility forms.
- Text without spaces, such as Chinese, Japanese, and Thai prose, comes back unbroken at any `columns`.
- `wrap` rejects `0`, a negative number, a fraction, `NaN`, `Infinity`, and an unsafe integer with `RangeError` and the sentence `Wrap width must be a positive safe integer.`, and `pad(wrap(text, n), n, { align: 'center' })` centers each line.
- Marked lanes: `info`, `success`, `warn`, `error`, `debug`, and `trace` wrap a long message at `columns` minus the measured glyph gutter where `columns` is defined and leave it unwrapped when no column remains after the gutter, continuation lines carry the gutter, authored line breaks keep their gutter, and `print` does not wrap.
- Golden fixtures that run without a terminal are byte for byte unchanged, for every lane, the table, the records view, and the lanes of an invocation by name.
- The update notice: on an 80-column stderr terminal the notice wraps with the info lane's gutter on its continuation line, and on a pipe it stays one line.
- Failure text: core's default text for each failure class stays one line per sentence on a terminal narrower than the sentence and on a pipe, and an override that calls `context.wrap` wraps its own text. A failure view override receives `columns`, `wrap`, and `expandTabs`. Help pages wrap under [Help wrapping acceptance](#help-wrapping-acceptance).
- The Developer Diagnostic's explanation breaks at stderr's effective width with the same line breaker as `context.wrap`, and a word wider than that width keeps its own line. On a 100-column stderr terminal the banner fills 100 columns and the explanation wraps at 100, and under `COLUMNS=60` they fill 60. With no width, they use 80, and so does a stderr that is not a terminal even when a host override reports a width. An explanation with wide characters wraps by display width, not by string length.

Process fixtures run on Node and Bun. Captured Windows facts test glyph selection; these fixtures do not certify native Windows support. Named-theme whole-token replacement belongs to [Loom theme acceptance](#loom-theme-acceptance). Fallback-option coverage belongs to [Fallback acceptance](#fallback-acceptance).
